Composables.summary: A composable is a reusable function built with Vue's Composition API. It packages stateful logic and can use reactive APIs, lifecycle hooks, and other composables.
Composables.explanation: A composable is a function that uses Vue's Composition API to package stateful logic for reuse. It can use refs, lifecycle hooks, watchers, and other composables, then return state or methods to a component.
Composables.syntax: function useFeature(input) { /* stateful logic */ return { state } }

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Optional input. A composable may accept a plain value, ref, or getter and normalize it with toValue().

Composables.returns: Usually a plain object containing refs, and possibly methods or other returned values.

example.title: A mouse-position composable
example.explanation: This composable stores the mouse position in refs, starts listening after mount, removes the listener during unmount, and returns the refs for use in a component.

useCases.title: Browser events
useCases.scenario: Track browser state such as mouse position while adding and removing listeners with the component lifecycle.

useCases.title: Async data
useCases.scenario: Handle loading, success, and error state around asynchronous data fetching.

useCases.title: Code organization
useCases.scenario: Split a large component into smaller units organized by logical features.

useCases.title: Logic reuse
useCases.scenario: Reuse pure logic without creating another component instance or visual layout.

interview.question: What is a Vue composable?
interview.answer: A composable is a function that uses the Composition API to package and reuse stateful logic. Each component instance that calls it normally gets its own state, so separate callers do not interfere.
interview.followUp: How would you share state instead? Use a shared state-management pattern rather than creating independent state inside each composable call.

interview.question: How should a composable return state?
interview.answer: Return a plain object containing refs. Consumers can destructure those refs and keep their reactive connection to the composable's state.
interview.followUp: What if property-style access is preferred? Wrap the returned object with reactive() so its refs are unwrapped as properties.

interview.question: How do you test a composable?
interview.answer: A composable that uses only reactivity APIs can be called directly in a unit test. If it uses lifecycle hooks or provide/inject, test it inside a mounted host component.
interview.followUp: What must the host test do for cleanup? Unmount the app so the composable's onUnmounted behavior runs.

keyPoints: Use composables to extract logic that owns changing state, such as mouse tracking or connection status.
Build larger features by letting one composable call smaller composables.
A normal composable call creates independent state for each component instance.
Return a plain object of refs so callers can destructure it without losing reactivity.
Track changing ref or getter inputs with watch(), or call toValue() inside watchEffect().
gotchas: In SSR apps, access the DOM only from post-mount hooks such as onMounted().
Remove event listeners and other effects when the component is unmounted.
Call composables from script setup or setup(), and normally call them synchronously there.
Returning reactive() directly can break reactivity when consumers destructure the result; return an object containing refs instead.

Composition API.summary: Composition API is a set of Vue APIs for writing component logic with imported functions. It combines reactive state, lifecycle hooks, and dependency injection, and is commonly used with <script setup> in Vue 3.
Composition API.explanation: Composition API lets a component use imported Vue functions for reactive state, lifecycle hooks, and dependency injection. In Vue 3, it is commonly used with <script setup>. The code runs once during setup, and Vue tracks reactive values used by computed properties and watchers.

parameters.name: props
parameters.description: The component props object passed as the first argument to setup().

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: The setup context, which can contain attrs, slots, emit, and expose.

Composition API.returns: When using setup(), return an object whose properties are exposed to the template and, when applicable, to the component instance. setup() may also return a render function.

example.title: Composition API counter
example.code:
<script setup>
import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
function increment() {
  count.value++
}

onMounted(() => {
  console.log(`Initial count: ${count.value}`)
})
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="increment">Count is: {{ count }}</button>
</template>
example.explanation: This component creates reactive state with ref(), changes it in a function, and runs code after mounting.

useCases.title: Reuse logic with composables
useCases.scenario: Several components need the same stateful behavior.

useCases.title: Group related code
useCases.scenario: A component handles several separate concerns.

useCases.title: Infer types with plain variables and functions
useCases.scenario: A project uses TypeScript.

useCases.title: Add Composition API incrementally
useCases.scenario: An existing Options API component needs a Composition API library.

interview.question: What is the Composition API?
interview.answer: Composition API is a group of Vue APIs for writing component logic with imported functions. It includes reactivity APIs, lifecycle hooks, and dependency injection.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from functional programming? It still uses Vue's mutable, fine-grained reactivity model, so function composition does not make it functional programming.

interview.question: Why use Composition API?
interview.answer: Its main benefit is reusable stateful logic through composable functions. It also lets related code stay together, which makes large components easier to refactor and maintain.
interview.followUp: Why can this help large components? A logical concern can be moved into an external utility without collecting code from several Options API sections.

interview.question: Can Composition API and Options API be used together?
interview.answer: Yes. Composition API can be used through setup() inside an Options API component. Vue recommends this mainly when an existing Options API codebase must use new Composition API features or libraries.
interview.followUp: Is Options API being removed? No. Vue documents it as an integral API and a good choice for many low- to medium-complexity cases.

keyPoints: The term includes reactivity functions such as ref() and reactive(), lifecycle hooks such as onMounted(), and provide()/inject().
Vue 3 includes it directly. Older Vue 2 releases need the official compatibility plugin.
Composable functions provide a way to reuse stateful logic without the main drawbacks of mixins.
This design supports strong TypeScript inference with few manual type annotations.
Using <script setup> can reduce runtime overhead and improve minification compared with equivalent Options API code.
Options API remains supported and is suitable for many components with low or medium complexity.
gotchas: Do not use this inside setup(); its value is undefined there.
An asynchronous setup() is supported only when the component is under Suspense.
Templates can read returned refs without .value, but JavaScript code still uses .value.

computed.summary: computed() creates a reactive value from a getter. Vue tracks its dependencies, caches the result, and recalculates it when those dependencies change.
computed.explanation: computed() runs a getter and returns a computed ref. Vue tracks the reactive values read by the getter, caches the result, and recalculates it only after a tracked dependency changes. In templates, the ref is automatically unwrapped, but JavaScript code reads the result with .value.
computed.syntax:
computed(getter, debuggerOptions?)
computed({ get, set }, debuggerOptions?)

parameters.name: getter or options
parameters.description: A function that calculates the value from reactive dependencies, or an options object with get and set functions.

parameters.name: debuggerOptions
parameters.description: Optional debugger callbacks for tracking and triggering.

computed.returns: A read-only computed ref for a getter, or a writable ref when get and set are supplied.

example.title: A read-only computed ref
example.explanation: The computed ref derives a value from count and updates after count changes.

useCases.title: Clean template logic
useCases.scenario: Move repeated or complex reactive calculations out of a template.

useCases.title: Cache derived data
useCases.scenario: Reuse an expensive calculation without running it on every render.

useCases.title: Writable derived value
useCases.scenario: Expose a value that can also update source state when assigned.

interview.question: What does computed() return, and how does it update?
interview.answer: computed() receives a getter and returns a computed ref. The getter reads reactive dependencies, and Vue tracks those reads so the result can update when they change.
interview.followUp: How does a computed ref differ from a method? A computed ref caches its result until a reactive dependency changes, while a method runs whenever a render invokes it.

interview.question: Why are computed properties cached?
interview.answer: A computed property evaluates its getter once for a dependency state and reuses that result for later reads. It evaluates again only after one of its reactive dependencies changes.
interview.followUp: When should a method be used instead? Use a method when caching is not wanted or when the calculation must run on each render.

interview.question: How do you create a writable computed ref?
interview.answer: A writable computed ref is created with an object containing get and set functions. Assigning to the computed ref calls set, which should update the underlying source state.
interview.followUp: What happens with a getter-only computed ref? Assigning to it produces a runtime warning because it has no setter.

keyPoints: Use a computed property when template logic becomes more complex and depends on reactive data.
Vue records the reactive values read by the getter and updates dependent bindings when those values change.
The Composition API form returns a computed ref. Read its value with .value in JavaScript.
Templates can use a computed ref without writing .value.
Repeated reads reuse the cached result until a dependency changes.
Pass a getter function for a read-only computed ref, or pass get and set functions for a writable one.
gotchas: A computed ref cannot be assigned directly unless it was created with both a getter and a setter.
Do not change other state, make asynchronous requests, or change the DOM inside a computed getter.
A computed value based only on Date.now() does not refresh because Date.now() is not reactive.
Treat the returned value as read-only. Change the source state instead of changing the computed result.

createApp.summary: createApp creates a Vue application instance from a root component and optional root props. Configure the app, then call mount to render it in a container.
createApp.explanation: Call createApp with a root component and optional props to get an application instance. Configure the instance, register assets, or install plugins before calling mount; mount returns the root component instance and can be called only once for that app.
createApp.syntax: function createApp(rootComponent: Component, rootProps?: object): App

parameters.name: rootComponent
parameters.description: The root component for the application.

parameters.name: rootProps
parameters.description: Optional props passed to the root component.

example.title: Create and mount an app
example.code:
import { createApp } from 'vue'
import App from './App.vue'

const app = createApp(App, { message: 'Hello' })
app.mount('#app')
example.explanation: This creates an app with App as its root component, passes it a prop, and mounts it into the element that matches #app.

useCases.title: Application startup
useCases.scenario: Start a Vue application from an imported single-file root component.

useCases.title: Initial root props
useCases.scenario: Pass initial values to the root component as props.

useCases.title: Multiple app instances
useCases.scenario: Create separate Vue apps for different page regions.

interview.question: What does createApp do, and when does rendering begin?
interview.answer: createApp creates an application instance from a root component and optional root props. The app does not render until mount is called.
interview.followUp: How can two Vue apps share a page safely? Create separate app instances and mount them on different containers; each app has its own configuration and global assets.

interview.question: What are the input and return value of app.mount()?
interview.answer: mount accepts a DOM element or a CSS selector. It returns the root component instance, not the application instance, and it can be called only once per app.
interview.followUp: What happens in SSR hydration mode? Vue hydrates the existing DOM in the container and adjusts mismatched nodes to match the expected output.

interview.question: How does app.use handle plugins and options?
interview.answer: app.use installs a plugin. The plugin can be an object with install or a function, and extra arguments are passed to the plugin installation.
interview.followUp: Where should application-wide dependencies be exposed? Use provide for values that descendant components can inject, or globalProperties when appropriate.

keyPoints: The optional second argument supplies props to the root component.
mount accepts either a DOM element or a selector string.
mount returns the root component instance.
directive registers a named directive; passing only its name retrieves the registered directive.
provide makes a value available for injection in descendant components within the app.
Each app has its own config object for application-level settings.
gotchas: Do not call mount more than once on the same application instance.
Finish configuration and registration before mounting.
Calling use repeatedly does not install the same plugin repeatedly.

createRouter.summary: createRouter() builds a Router instance for a Vue app. Pass RouterOptions, including routes and a history implementation.
createRouter.explanation: Call createRouter with RouterOptions to build the router used by a Vue app. The options include a history implementation and route records. The router can then be installed on the app with app.use(router).

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: RouterOptions used to initialize the Router instance.

example.title: Create a Vue Router instance
example.explanation: This creates a router with browser history and one route.

useCases.title: Create normal browser routing with createWebHistory.
useCases.scenario: Browser single-page application

useCases.title: Use hash routing with createWebHashHistory.
useCases.scenario: Static hosting or unsupported server rewrites

useCases.title: Use memory history with createMemoryHistory on the server.
useCases.scenario: Server-side rendering

interview.question: What does createRouter do?
interview.answer: createRouter creates the Router instance used by a Vue app. Its argument is a RouterOptions object, and the function returns the router.
interview.followUp: How do you choose history? Use createWebHistory for normal single-page apps, createWebHashHistory when the server cannot handle arbitrary URLs, and createMemoryHistory for SSR or memory-only use.

interview.question: Which option is required?
interview.answer: The options must include routes. The router is designed to start with route records, although more routes can be added later.
interview.followUp: What happens with a named route that does not exist? Calling push or resolve with that name throws an error.

interview.question: How is navigation history configured?
interview.answer: The history option replaces the old mode option. It receives a history object created by a function such as createWebHistory.
interview.followUp: Where is the base path configured? Pass it as the first argument to the selected history creator.

keyPoints: The function creates the router object that a Vue application can use.
Its signature accepts one options object and returns a router instance.
RouterOptions describes the settings used to initialize the router.
createWebHistory is the usual choice for a browser-based single-page app.
createWebHashHistory is useful when the app has no host or the server cannot handle every URL.
createMemoryHistory is intended mainly for server-side rendering.
gotchas: Pass a routes array when creating the router, even if you plan to add routes later.
For server-side rendering, use createMemoryHistory on the server and a browser history in the client.
Set the application base path on the history function, not as a createRouter option.

defineAsyncComponent.summary: defineAsyncComponent lets Vue load a component only when it is rendered. It accepts a Promise-returning loader and can show loading or error components while loading.
defineAsyncComponent.explanation: defineAsyncComponent creates a wrapper around a component loader. The loader returns a Promise, often from a dynamic import. Vue calls it when the wrapper is rendered, then forwards props and slots to the loaded component. An options object can add loading and error components, delays, timeouts, retry handling, and other loading behavior.

parameters.name: source / loader
parameters.description: A function that returns a Promise resolving to the component.

parameters.name: loader
parameters.description: The component loader used by the options form.

parameters.name: loadingComponent
parameters.description: Component shown while loading.

parameters.name: errorComponent
parameters.description: Component shown when loading fails.

parameters.name: delay
parameters.description: Delay before showing the loading component.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum loading time before failure.

parameters.name: suspensible
parameters.description: Whether the async component can integrate with Suspense.

parameters.name: onError
parameters.type: (error: Error, retry: () => void, fail: () => void, attempts: number) => any | undefined
parameters.description: Called after an error; receives retry, fail, and the attempt count.

defineAsyncComponent.returns: A component wrapper that lazy-loads the resolved component.

example.title: Lazy-load a component
example.explanation: The component is loaded when Vue renders UserPanel.

useCases.title: Lazy-load feature components
useCases.scenario: Split a large application into smaller chunks and load a feature only when the feature is rendered.

useCases.title: Display loading UI
useCases.scenario: Show a temporary placeholder while a slow component loads.

useCases.title: Handle loading errors
useCases.scenario: Show fallback UI or retry a failed component request.

interview.question: What does defineAsyncComponent accept?
interview.answer: defineAsyncComponent accepts either a loader function or an options object. The loader must return a Promise that resolves to a component.
interview.followUp: What does the wrapper do after loading? It forwards the original component's props and slots, so it can replace the normal component while loading it lazily.

interview.question: Why is dynamic import commonly used with async components?
interview.answer: A dynamic import returns a Promise, so it can be passed directly as the loader. Bundlers can use the import as a split point for a separate chunk.
interview.followUp: When does the loader run? The wrapper calls it when the async component is actually rendered, not merely when it is declared.

interview.question: How can loading and failure behavior be customized?
interview.answer: The options form uses loader and can also define loadingComponent, errorComponent, delay, timeout, suspensible, and onError. The onError callback receives the error, retry and fail functions, and the attempt count.
interview.followUp: How can a failed load be handled? Call retry to try loading again or fail to stop retrying; the attempt count allows bounded retry logic.

keyPoints: The simple form takes a function whose result is a Promise for the component.
Loading is lazy: Vue starts the loader when the wrapper is rendered.
The wrapper preserves the normal component interface by forwarding props and slots.
A dynamic import works with common bundlers and can create a separate bundle chunk.
You can register an async component globally with the normal app.component API.
The helper also works in a local components registration object.
gotchas: In Vue 3, wrap the loader with defineAsyncComponent. Do not use a bare function that returns a Promise as the component definition.
Vue Router has its own lazy-loading mechanism for route components. Use that mechanism instead of defineAsyncComponent for routes.

defineComponent.summary: defineComponent() is a Vue type helper. It improves TypeScript inference for components, including props, setup context, and component instances.
defineComponent.explanation: defineComponent() helps TypeScript infer a Vue component's types. It returns the component options or a render-function component and does not add runtime behavior for the options form.
defineComponent.syntax:
function defineComponent(component: ComponentOptions): ComponentConstructor
function defineComponent(setup: ComponentOptions['setup'], extraOptions?: ComponentOptions): () => any

parameters.name: component / setup
parameters.description: A Vue component options object, or a setup-like function that returns a render function.

parameters.name: extraOptions
parameters.description: Optional component options used with the function form, such as props or emits.

defineComponent.returns: A typed component constructor for the options form, or a component function for the function form.

example.title: Function-form component
example.explanation: This component uses the function form of defineComponent. It creates reactive state and returns a render function.

useCases.title: Type component options
useCases.scenario: A component uses the Options API and needs reliable TypeScript inference.

useCases.title: Create render-function components
useCases.scenario: A TypeScript or TSX component returns a render function.

useCases.title: Extract an instance type
useCases.scenario: Code needs the inferred type of a component instance.

interview.question: What is the main purpose of defineComponent()?
interview.answer: defineComponent() is a type helper. In the options form, it returns the same options object at runtime while improving component type inference.
interview.followUp: How can you get the component instance type? Use InstanceType<typeof Foo> when Foo is the result of defineComponent().

interview.question: How does the function form differ from the options form?
interview.answer: The function form receives props and the setup context, then returns a render function. It supports both h() and JSX and is available from Vue 3.3.
interview.followUp: What must still be declared manually? Runtime props, and other extra options such as emits, still need explicit declarations.

interview.question: How does defineComponent() affect tree-shaking?
interview.answer: defineComponent() is normally side-effect-free, but webpack may not infer that from the function call. Add /*#__PURE__*/ before the call to allow tree-shaking.
interview.followUp: Is the annotation needed with Vite? No. The Rollup-based production bundler used by Vite can identify the call as side-effect-free.

keyPoints: Use it when TypeScript needs help inferring a component's props, setup context, or instance type.
The options form keeps the original options object at runtime; its main role is type inference.
The returned type can represent the component constructor and its inferred instance.
The function form is useful for TypeScript components that use render functions or TSX.
A function-form component may render with either h() or JSX.
gotchas: The function signature is available only from Vue 3.3 onward.
With the function form, declare runtime props manually when the component needs them.
For webpack tree-shaking, add a /*#__PURE__*/ annotation before the call if an unused component must be removable.

defineEmits.summary: defineEmits declares the custom events a Vue component can emit. In <script setup>, it returns a function for sending events with optional payloads and type checking.
defineEmits.explanation: defineEmits declares the custom events a component can send. In <script setup>, it returns an emit function for sending an event and its payload. You can declare events with runtime values or TypeScript types, but not both forms together.

parameters.name: emits
parameters.description: Runtime declaration: an array of event names, or an object mapping event names to validator functions.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Type-only declaration describing event names and their payload argument types.

defineEmits.returns: A function that emits a declared component event. The function accepts the event name and any payload arguments.

example.title: Declare and emit an event
example.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
const emit = defineEmits<{
  submit: [email: string, password: string]
}>()

function submitForm() {
  emit('submit', 'user@example.com', 'secret')
}
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="submitForm">Submit</button>
</template>
example.explanation: This component declares a typed submit event and emits it when the button is clicked.

useCases.title: Send a custom event
useCases.scenario: A child component needs to notify its parent that an action happened.

useCases.title: Type event arguments
useCases.scenario: A component needs typed payloads in a TypeScript project.

useCases.title: Validate event payloads
useCases.scenario: A component should check event data at runtime.

interview.question: What is defineEmits used for?
interview.answer: defineEmits is a compiler macro used in <script setup> to declare component events. It can return a function that sends those events.
interview.followUp: Can it be imported? No. Vue makes it available automatically and removes it during compilation.

interview.question: How can events and payloads be declared?
interview.answer: It accepts an event-name array, an object with optional validators, or a TypeScript type declaration. The type form can describe event names and payload types.
interview.followUp: What happens if runtime and type declarations are both supplied? Vue reports a compile error.

interview.question: How does a component send an event?
interview.answer: The returned emit function takes the event name followed by payload arguments. A parent listens with a component event listener such as @submit.
interview.followUp: How can invalid payloads be checked at runtime? Use object syntax and return true or false from the event validator.

keyPoints: In <script setup>, call the function returned by defineEmits to send an event from component code.
Runtime declarations can use an array of event names or an object with event validators.
Arguments after the event name become the payload received by the parent listener.
With TypeScript, a type declaration can describe event payloads using call signatures or named tuples.
Declaring events records the component's event contract and can add payload validation.
gotchas: Use defineEmits only directly inside <script setup>. Do not call it inside another function or a normal script block.
Choose either runtime syntax or type-only syntax for one declaration. Combining them causes a compile error.
Declarations are moved to module scope, so they cannot use local setup variables. Imported bindings are allowed.

defineExpose.summary: `defineExpose()` controls which bindings in a `<script setup>` component a parent can access through a template ref. The component is private by default, so only explicitly exposed properties and methods are public.
defineExpose.explanation: `defineExpose()` declares which bindings from `<script setup>` are available through a parent template ref or a `$parent` chain. Components using `<script setup>` hide their bindings unless this macro exposes them. Exposed refs are automatically unwrapped on the public component instance.

parameters.name: exposed
parameters.description: An object containing the properties and methods that should be public on the component instance.

defineExpose.returns: No runtime return value is documented; the macro defines the component's public instance interface.

example.title: Expose a component value
example.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
defineExpose({ count })
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="count++">{{ count }}</button>
</template>
example.explanation: This component exposes its count ref to a parent using a template ref. The parent receives the ref value without needing to unwrap it.

useCases.title: Provide controlled instance access
useCases.scenario: Expose a small public API such as `open()` or `focus()` for a parent component.

useCases.title: Share selected state
useCases.scenario: Allow a parent with a template ref to read selected component state.

interview.question: What does `defineExpose()` do?
interview.answer: `defineExpose()` is a compiler macro for choosing the public bindings of a component that uses `<script setup>`. A parent can read those bindings through a template ref. Without it, the component instance does not expose the setup bindings.
interview.followUp: What happens to an exposed ref? The public instance automatically unwraps it, so a ref such as `ref(2)` appears as a number to the parent.

interview.question: What is the default visibility of `<script setup>` bindings?
interview.answer: A component using `<script setup>` is closed by default. Its local variables and functions are not available to a parent through a template ref unless they are included in the object passed to `defineExpose()`.
interview.followUp: How should normal parent-child communication usually work? Prefer props and emitted events, and use component refs only when direct instance access is needed.

interview.question: What timing rule applies to `defineExpose()`?
interview.answer: Call `defineExpose()` before any `await` operation in the setup code. Bindings exposed after an await are not accessible through the component instance.
interview.followUp: Can the macro be imported? No. It is recognized by the Vue SFC compiler and does not need an import.

keyPoints: Pass an object to `defineExpose()` to publish selected variables or methods.
A parent accesses the exposed public interface through a template ref.
Exposed refs appear as their inner values on the public instance.
The exposed interface is visible through template refs and `$parent` chains.
The public instance contains the properties included in the object passed to the macro.
gotchas: Bindings in `<script setup>` are private unless they are explicitly passed to `defineExpose()`.
Call the macro before the first `await`; values exposed after that point will not be available.
Do not import `defineExpose` from Vue. The SFC compiler provides it as a macro.

defineModel.summary: defineModel() is a Vue 3.4+ <script setup> macro for component v-model. It gives the child a ref that reads and updates the parent's bound value.
defineModel.explanation: In <script setup>, defineModel() creates a ref connected to the parent component's v-model. Reading it gets the parent's value. Changing it sends the new value back to the parent. The compiler represents this connection with a modelValue prop and an update:modelValue event.
defineModel.syntax:
const model = defineModel<T>(options?)
const namedModel = defineModel<T>('name', options?)

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional model configuration, such as required or default.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Optional model name used for a named v-model.

defineModel.returns: A ref that is synchronized with the parent v-model. defineModel() can also expose a modifiers object when its return value is destructured.

example.title: A component model
example.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
const count = defineModel<number>({ default: 0 })
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="count++">Count: {{ count }}</button>
</template>
example.explanation: This child component exposes a model value. A parent can bind it with <Counter v-model="count" />.

useCases.title: Connect a component model to an input with v-model.
useCases.scenario: Wrap a native input

useCases.title: Let a child read and change a parent value.
useCases.scenario: Expose one value

useCases.title: Use named models for separate fields such as first and last name.
useCases.scenario: Expose several values

useCases.title: Read modifiers and apply custom get or set behavior.
useCases.scenario: Transform input values

interview.question: What does defineModel() do?
interview.answer: defineModel() returns a ref for the component's v-model. Its value follows the parent binding, and changing the ref updates the parent.
interview.followUp: What does the compiler generate? It uses a modelValue prop and an update:modelValue event.

interview.question: How do you create multiple v-model bindings?
interview.answer: A named model uses defineModel('firstName') and matches v-model:first-name in the parent. Each named model has its own prop and update event.
interview.followUp: How can one model use a modifier? Destructure the return value and inspect its modifiers object.

interview.question: How are component v-model modifiers handled?
interview.answer: Modifiers are available by destructuring defineModel() into a model ref and a modifiers object. The object reports enabled modifiers, such as capitalize.
interview.followUp: How can a modifier change the value? Pass get and set options to defineModel and apply the modifier in the setter.

keyPoints: Use defineModel() in Vue 3.4 and later for the usual component v-model pattern.
The returned value is a ref, so use its value in script and bind it directly in a template.
Changing the model in the child sends the new value to the parent.
The macro connects the local ref to a modelValue prop.
The child update is communicated with the update:modelValue event.
Named models let one component synchronize several independent values.
gotchas: A default model value can become different from the parent's value when the parent does not provide a value.

defineProps.summary: defineProps declares the props a Vue component accepts. It supports runtime options or a TypeScript type declaration and returns the received props for use in script.
defineProps.explanation: defineProps declares the props that a component accepts. In script setup, Vue exposes declared props to the template, and the macro also returns the props object for JavaScript access. You can use runtime options or a TypeScript type declaration, but not both in one call.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Runtime prop options: an array of names or an object with types, defaults, and validators.

parameters.name: Props
parameters.description: Optional TypeScript type describing the component props.

defineProps.returns: A props object containing the values passed to the component; declared props are also available in the template.

example.title: Declare a typed prop
example.explanation: This component declares a required string prop named title and displays it in the template.

useCases.title: Accept parent data
useCases.scenario: A reusable component needs data from its parent, such as a title or selected item.

useCases.title: Validate prop values
useCases.scenario: A component should warn during development when a caller passes the wrong value type.

useCases.title: Declare typed props
useCases.scenario: A component needs a typed public interface in a TypeScript project.

useCases.title: Set default values
useCases.scenario: A prop needs a fallback when the parent omits it.

interview.question: What does defineProps do?
interview.answer: defineProps is a compiler macro for declaring component props inside script setup. It needs no import, and Vue makes declared props available in the template.
interview.followUp: How can props be typed? Use a runtime declaration such as { title: String } or a type argument such as defineProps<{ title: string }>(). Do not combine both forms.

interview.question: How do you access props in script setup?
interview.answer: The returned object contains the values passed by the parent, so JavaScript can read props.title. The template can also use the declared prop directly.
interview.followUp: What happens when a destructured prop is passed to watch? Pass a getter such as () => foo so Vue keeps tracking the prop.

interview.question: Can a child mutate a prop?
interview.answer: Props flow from parent to child. When the parent changes a prop, the child receives the new value, but the child cannot replace the prop binding.
interview.followUp: How should a child request a change? It should emit an event and let the parent perform the state update.

keyPoints: Use defineProps only inside a Vue SFC's script setup block. It is removed during compilation and does not need an import.
Store the return value when script code needs to read a prop, for example const props = defineProps(['title']).
The same prop declaration API also works outside script setup through the component's props option.
Object syntax can document and check expected types, such as { title: String, likes: Number }.
Reading props.foo in a computed value or watcher makes that prop a reactive dependency.
gotchas: A child component must not assign to a prop. Ask the parent to change the value instead.
The runtime options cannot use variables declared locally in the same setup scope.

defineSlots.summary: defineSlots() is a Vue <script setup> macro for typing slot names and slot props. It returns the component's slots object and takes no runtime arguments.
defineSlots.explanation: defineSlots() is a compile-time macro for describing slot names and slot props in TypeScript. Vue uses the type to give template tooling better checks and returns the component's slots object for script use.

parameters.name: type parameter
parameters.description: A TypeScript type literal whose keys are slot names and whose slot-function first parameters describe slot props.

defineSlots.returns: The component's slots object, equivalent to the slots object exposed on the setup context or returned by useSlots().

example.title: Type a slot with defineSlots
example.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
const slots = defineSlots<{
  default(props: { msg: string }): any
}>()
</script>

<template>
  <slot msg="Hello" />
</template>
example.explanation: Declares the default slot and the props it accepts. The returned slots object can also be used in script.

useCases.title: Type named slots
useCases.scenario: A component exposes named slots with documented props.

useCases.title: Improve template hints
useCases.scenario: A template uses slot props and needs IDE type checking.

useCases.title: Read slots in script
useCases.scenario: Script code needs access to the component's slots object.

interview.question: What is defineSlots() used for?
interview.answer: defineSlots() is a compile-time macro used in <script setup> to describe slot names and their props. It has no runtime arguments and provides type information for IDEs and template checking.
interview.followUp: What does it return? It returns a slots object equivalent to the object from useSlots(), so script code can call or inspect the declared slots.

interview.question: How do you declare slot props?
interview.answer: The type argument is a type literal. Each property name is a slot name, and each property value is a slot function whose first parameter describes the slot props.
interview.followUp: How are slot props exposed in the template? The parameter type becomes the type information available when using that slot's props.

interview.question: Does defineSlots() change runtime behavior?
interview.answer: defineSlots() is mainly a type hint and does not create runtime behavior. Its return value gives access to the component's slots object, while the slot return type is currently ignored.
interview.followUp: Which helper is the alternative when TypeScript slot hints are not needed? useSlots() returns the slots object directly from the setup context.

keyPoints: Use it to declare slot names and the types of props passed to those slots.
Write one property for each slot, using the property key as the slot name.
Describe slot props as the first parameter of the slot function type.
The macro returns the component's slots object for use in script code.
gotchas: Pass a type parameter only. Do not pass runtime values to defineSlots().
The slot function return type is not checked yet, so using any is currently acceptable.
The type declaration does not currently make IDE tools require a slot that is marked as required.

defineStore.summary: defineStore creates a function for retrieving a Pinia store. Give it a unique id and define the store with either options or a setup function.
defineStore.explanation: Call defineStore with a unique string and either an options object or a setup function. The returned useStore function creates or retrieves the store when called in a component setup context.
defineStore.syntax:
function defineStore<Id, S, G, A>(id, options): StoreDefinition<Id, S, G, A>
function defineStore<Id, SS>(id, storeSetup, options?): SetupStoreDefinition<Id, SS>

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: A unique string id for the store.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: An options object containing store options.

parameters.name: storeSetup
parameters.description: A function that defines and returns a setup store.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional extra options for a setup store.

defineStore.returns: A StoreDefinition or SetupStoreDefinition. The returned function retrieves the store instance.

example.title: A setup store
example.explanation: This setup store exposes reactive state, a computed value, and a method.

useCases.title: Create an application store
useCases.scenario: Use state, computed values, and methods in one shared module.

useCases.title: Build a flexible setup store
useCases.scenario: Use watchers or Vue composables inside a store.

useCases.title: Organize stores by file
useCases.scenario: Keep store definitions separate for bundling and type inference.

interview.question: What does defineStore do?
interview.answer: defineStore creates a useStore function. Its first argument is a unique store id, and its second argument is either an options object or a setup function.
interview.followUp: How can a store use application-provided values? A setup store can call inject() or use composables such as useRoute(), but those external values should not be returned as store properties.

interview.question: How do option stores and setup stores differ?
interview.answer: An option store has state, getters, and actions. State is the store data, getters act like computed values, and actions contain methods.
interview.followUp: When might setup syntax be preferable? It provides more flexibility, including watchers and free use of composables, although composables can be more complex with SSR.

interview.question: When is a Pinia store created?
interview.answer: The store is instantiated by calling its returned useStore function, commonly inside a component's script setup or setup function. After that, state, getters, and actions are available on the store object.
interview.followUp: How should stores be organized? Defining each store in a separate file can support code splitting and TypeScript inference.

keyPoints: The first argument is the store's unique id. Pinia uses it to connect the store with devtools.
The second argument can be an options object or a setup function.
In an option store, state holds data, getters provide computed values, and actions provide methods.
A setup store returns the reactive properties and methods that it exposes.
Separate store files can help bundlers split code and can provide TypeScript inference.
gotchas: The store is reactive, so access getters directly without .value. Destructuring the store directly can break reactivity; use storeToRefs for state and getters.
A router, route, or injected application value can be used inside a setup store, but should not be returned as store state.

h.summary: Vue's h function creates virtual DOM nodes. It accepts an element or component type, optional props, and optional children or slots.
h.explanation: Import h from Vue and call it in a render function to create a virtual node. Pass an HTML tag or component first, props second, and children third. For component vnodes, provide slots as functions.
h.syntax:
function h(type: string | Component, props?: object | null, children?: Children | Slot | Slots): VNode
function h(type: string | Component, children?: Children | Slot): VNode

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: A native element name or Vue component definition.

parameters.name: props
parameters.description: Optional props passed to the vnode.

parameters.name: children
parameters.description: Optional child content, a slot function, or named slot functions.

example.title: Create a button vnode
example.explanation: This render function creates a button vnode with a class, a click handler, and text content.

useCases.title: Programmatic rendering
useCases.scenario: Use JavaScript logic to build a UI when a template is not enough.

useCases.title: Native element rendering
useCases.scenario: Create an element vnode with attributes, events, and child content.

useCases.title: Component slots
useCases.scenario: Build a component vnode with default or named slots.

interview.question: What does Vue's h function do?
interview.answer: h creates virtual DOM nodes, called vnodes. Its first argument identifies a native element or Vue component, followed by optional props and children.
interview.followUp: How are component slots passed? Use a slot function for one default slot, or an object whose values are slot functions for named slots.

interview.question: What are the arguments and return value of h?
interview.answer: The first argument can be a string such as 'div' for a native element, or a component definition. The returned value is a VNode.
interview.followUp: What can the children value contain? It can be text, numbers, booleans, vnodes, null, or arrays of these values.

interview.question: How does h handle component slots?
interview.answer: For a component vnode, pass slot functions as children. A single function represents the default slot; an object maps slot names to slot functions.
interview.followUp: Why use render functions instead of templates? They provide programmatic JavaScript control when templates are not sufficient.

keyPoints: h creates virtual DOM nodes that Vue can render.
The type argument can name a native HTML element or identify a Vue component.
The optional props argument carries values such as attributes, classes, and event handlers; children come after it.
The name h is a short convention for a function that produces HTML-like virtual nodes.
For a component with only a default slot, pass one slot function directly.
gotchas: Component children are not ordinary child values. Pass them as slot functions.
You may omit props only when the next argument is a valid children value.

inject.summary: `inject()` gets a dependency provided by an ancestor or the app. It looks up the value by a string or Symbol key and can use a default when no provider exists.
inject.explanation: `inject()` finds a value supplied by an ancestor component or by the app. It searches by a string or Symbol key. If the value is a ref, Vue returns the ref unchanged, so the link to the provider stays reactive. The call must run synchronously in `setup()` or `<script setup>`.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key used to find the provided value. It can be a string or a Symbol.

parameters.name: defaultValue
parameters.description: Optional fallback returned when no matching provider exists. It can also be a factory when the third argument is true.

parameters.name: treatDefaultAsFactory
parameters.description: Optional flag that treats `defaultValue` as a factory function.

inject.returns: The provided value, or the default value when no provider matches. If neither exists, the result is undefined.

example.title: Inject a provided value
example.explanation: The component reads the value provided by an ancestor. It uses a shared Symbol key and a fallback value.

useCases.title: Avoid prop drilling
useCases.scenario: A deeply nested component needs shared data without passing props through every intermediate component.

useCases.title: Share app-level dependencies
useCases.scenario: A plugin or application-wide service must be available to all rendered components.

useCases.title: Use Symbol-based keys
useCases.scenario: A component library needs stable dependency keys that are unlikely to conflict.

interview.question: How does `inject()` find a value?
interview.answer: `inject()` looks up a value by a string or Symbol key in ancestor providers. The nearest matching provider in the parent chain supplies the value. An app-level provider is available to all components in that app.
interview.followUp: How can a component keep the value reactive? Provide a ref or reactive object. A provided ref is injected unchanged, preserving its reactive connection.

interview.question: How do default values work?
interview.answer: The call takes an injection key and can take a default value. The default is used when no provider matches the key. A factory can create an expensive or per-instance default only when needed.
interview.followUp: When is the factory form needed? Use `inject(key, factory, true)` when the second argument should be called to create the default.

interview.question: When should you use object syntax or Symbol keys?
interview.answer: Use the object form when the local property name differs from the provider key. Its `from` field names the source key, and its `default` field supplies a fallback. Symbol keys help avoid collisions in large applications.
interview.followUp: How should an injector update shared state? Prefer providing a mutation function with the state, or expose a readonly value to prevent injector mutation.

keyPoints: `inject(key)` reads the dependency identified by `key`; the key can be a string or a Symbol.
Use the Composition API function inside `<script setup>` or synchronously inside `setup()`.
An app can provide a shared value for every component it renders.
Pass `true` as the third argument when the default argument is a factory function.
Export shared Symbol keys from a dedicated file so providers and injectors use the same identity.
gotchas: A provided ref stays a ref after injection. Read or change its `.value` in JavaScript.

isRef.summary: isRef() checks whether a value is a Vue ref. In TypeScript, a successful check narrows the value to Ref<unknown>, so code can safely use .value.
isRef.explanation: isRef() checks whether a value is a Vue ref object. Its type-predicate return value also narrows an unknown value to Ref<unknown>, so TypeScript allows access to .value inside the condition.
isRef.syntax: function isRef<T>(r: Ref<T> | unknown): r is Ref<T>

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: The value to test. It may be a Ref<T> or any unknown value.

isRef.returns: A boolean result. In TypeScript, the result is a type predicate: r is Ref<T>.

example.title: Check whether a value is a ref
example.explanation: This checks an unknown value before using its reactive value property.

useCases.title: Handle ref-or-value inputs
useCases.scenario: A utility accepts either a plain value or a ref and needs to handle ref values directly.

useCases.title: Safely inspect unknown data
useCases.scenario: An unknown value must be checked before reading its reactive value.

interview.question: What does isRef() do?
interview.answer: isRef() returns true when the value is a ref object. It returns false for values that are not refs.
interview.followUp: Why is its return type useful in TypeScript? It acts as a type guard, narrowing the checked value to Ref<unknown>.

interview.question: When would you use isRef() in a function?
interview.answer: Use isRef() when a function accepts either a plain value or a ref. After the check, code can safely read or change .value.
interview.followUp: What helper reads either form without an explicit check? unref() returns .value for refs and returns plain values unchanged.

interview.question: How does isRef() support TypeScript?
interview.answer: The function takes Ref<T> or unknown and returns a type predicate: r is Ref<T>. This lets TypeScript narrow the value after a true result.
interview.followUp: What happens if the input is a plain value? The check is false, so the value is not narrowed to a ref.

keyPoints: isRef() tests whether a value is a ref object.
Its type-predicate return value lets TypeScript use isRef() as a type guard.
After a successful check on an unknown value, TypeScript narrows it to Ref<unknown>.

KeepAlive.summary: KeepAlive caches inactive dynamic components so their state survives when users switch between views. It can filter cached components by name and limit the cache size.
KeepAlive.explanation: KeepAlive stores inactive component instances instead of destroying them when a dynamic component changes. When a cached component returns, Vue activates the existing instance. When it leaves, Vue deactivates it. You can filter cached components by name and limit the cache size.

parameters.name: include
parameters.description: A string, regular expression, or array of strings and regular expressions that selects component names to cache.

parameters.name: exclude
parameters.description: A string, regular expression, or array of strings and regular expressions that excludes matching component names from caching.

parameters.name: max
parameters.description: The maximum number of component instances to cache.

example.title: Cache dynamic components
example.code:
<KeepAlive :max="10">
  <component :is="activeComponent" />
</KeepAlive>
example.explanation: The active component changes without losing cached component state. At most 10 component instances stay cached.

useCases.title: Preserve view state
useCases.scenario: Switching between tabs or views

useCases.title: Control what is cached
useCases.scenario: Caching only selected named components

useCases.title: Limit cached instances
useCases.scenario: Bounding memory and cache growth

interview.question: What problem does KeepAlive solve?
interview.answer: KeepAlive caches inactive component instances instead of unmounting them. This preserves their state when a dynamic component is shown again.
interview.followUp: What happens when a cached component leaves the DOM? It enters a deactivated state, and its deactivated hook runs.

interview.question: How do include and exclude work?
interview.answer: include selects components whose names match a string, regular expression, or array. exclude prevents matching components from being cached.
interview.followUp: What does matching use? Vue checks the component's name option, so the component needs a name for conditional caching.

interview.question: What does the max prop do?
interview.answer: The max prop limits the number of cached instances. When the limit is reached, KeepAlive removes the least recently accessed cached instance.
interview.followUp: What kind of cache policy is this? It is an LRU policy, so recent access keeps an instance in the cache.

keyPoints: KeepAlive preserves inactive dynamic component instances instead of destroying them.
Only one active component instance can be the direct child of KeepAlive at a time.
The include prop restricts caching to components whose names match its pattern.
The exclude prop prevents matching named components from entering the cache.
The max prop sets the maximum number of cached component instances.
Cached components use activated and deactivated lifecycle hooks when they enter or leave the cached state.
gotchas: include and exclude match component names. A component must have a name for name-based caching. With script setup, Vue can infer the name from the file name since version 3.2.34.
A KeepAlive direct child must render only one active component at a time, including when using v-if and v-else branches.

nextTick.summary: Vue's nextTick waits for pending DOM updates after reactive state changes. Use it when code needs to work with the updated DOM.
nextTick.explanation: Vue batches DOM changes after reactive state changes. Call nextTick after the change when code must use the updated DOM, either by awaiting its Promise or by passing a callback.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: An optional function called after the pending DOM update flush.

nextTick.returns: Promise<void>, resolved after the pending DOM updates complete.

example.title: Wait for a DOM update
example.explanation: After changing the reactive value, wait for nextTick before reading the updated DOM.

useCases.title: Inspect updated DOM
useCases.scenario: Read an element's text, size, or other DOM state after changing reactive data.

useCases.title: Act after rendering
useCases.scenario: Run code that depends on Vue finishing its buffered render work.

interview.question: What does nextTick do?
interview.answer: nextTick waits until Vue finishes applying buffered DOM updates caused by reactive state changes. It returns a Promise, so an async function can use await nextTick().
interview.followUp: Why does Vue buffer these updates? It batches changes so each component updates only once even when several state changes occur.

interview.question: When should you use nextTick?
interview.answer: Call it after changing reactive state when code must inspect or use the updated DOM. Reading the DOM before the wait can still return the old content.
interview.followUp: What can you use instead of await? Pass a callback to nextTick(callback), which runs after the update flush.

interview.question: What is the nextTick signature and return value?
interview.answer: Its signature is nextTick(callback?: () => void): Promise<void>. The callback is optional, and the returned Promise resolves after the DOM updates complete.
interview.followUp: Can nextTick be used without a callback? Yes. Awaiting the returned Promise is the documented alternative.

keyPoints: nextTick is a Vue utility for waiting until the next DOM update flush finishes.
A reactive state mutation does not update the DOM immediately.
Vue buffers DOM work until the next tick.
Buffering lets each component update once even after multiple state changes.
Use nextTick immediately after the state change when later code needs the completed DOM update.
gotchas: Do not read the DOM immediately after changing reactive state when you need the new result.
Use either the callback form or await the Promise; both wait for the DOM update flush.

onBeforeMount.summary: onBeforeMount() runs before Vue creates a component's DOM. onMounted() runs after the component DOM and its synchronous children are mounted.
onBeforeMount.explanation: Call onBeforeMount() when setup is complete but the component has no DOM nodes yet. Call onMounted() when the component DOM and synchronous child components are ready. Register both calls synchronously inside setup(), usually in <script setup>.
onBeforeMount.syntax:
function onBeforeMount(callback: () => void, target?: ComponentInternalInstance | null): void
function onMounted(callback: () => void, target?: ComponentInternalInstance | null): void

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Function called at the selected lifecycle point.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: Optional component instance that receives the hook.

example.title: Run code at component mount time
example.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { onBeforeMount, onMounted } from 'vue'

onBeforeMount(() => {
  console.log('before the first DOM render')
})

onMounted(() => {
  console.log('the component DOM is ready')
})
</script>

<template>
  <button>Save</button>
</template>
example.explanation: The first callback runs before Vue creates the component's DOM. The second runs after the component's DOM and synchronous children are mounted.

useCases.title: Use rendered DOM
useCases.scenario: A component needs to measure, focus, or otherwise access elements after rendering.

useCases.title: Start client-side effects
useCases.scenario: A component starts a browser-side effect such as a timer or event listener.

useCases.title: Prepare before mounting
useCases.scenario: A component needs code immediately before its first DOM render.

interview.question: What is the difference between onBeforeMount() and onMounted()?
interview.answer: onBeforeMount() runs after the component has prepared its reactive state but before Vue creates its DOM nodes. onMounted() runs after the component DOM is inserted and all synchronous child components are mounted.
interview.followUp: Does onMounted() always mean the DOM is in the document? Only when the application's root container is also in the document.

interview.question: When would you use onMounted()?
interview.answer: Use onMounted() for side effects that need the rendered DOM, such as client-only DOM work. Use onBeforeMount() when code must run just before the first DOM render.
interview.followUp: What should browser-only code do during server rendering? Move it to a client-only lifecycle hook such as onMounted(), or otherwise prevent it from running on the server.

interview.question: When must these hooks be registered?
interview.answer: Lifecycle APIs must be called synchronously during a component's setup() phase. A callback is then invoked at the lifecycle point described by that hook.
interview.followUp: Can onMounted() be used to wait for async components? No. The mounted guarantee excludes async components and components inside Suspense trees.

keyPoints: onMounted(callback) schedules callback after the component has mounted.
The mounted point includes all synchronous child components.
At mount time, the component's DOM tree exists and is inserted into its parent container.
Use onMounted() for effects that need to read or change rendered DOM.
onBeforeMount() runs immediately before the component mounts.
Before onBeforeMount() runs, reactive state is ready but the component has no DOM nodes.
gotchas: Register these lifecycle hooks synchronously during setup(); calling them later is not supported.
onBeforeMount() and onMounted() do not run during server-side rendering, so server-rendered code must not depend on them.
onMounted() does not wait for asynchronous components or components inside Suspense trees.

onBeforeUnmount.summary: `onBeforeUnmount()` registers a callback that Vue runs just before a component is unmounted. The component is still fully functional at that time.
onBeforeUnmount.explanation: Call `onBeforeUnmount()` during `setup()` to register cleanup code. Vue runs the callback immediately before the component is unmounted, while the component is still fully functional.
onBeforeUnmount.syntax: function onBeforeUnmount(callback: () => void, target?: ComponentInternalInstance | null): void

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Function called immediately before the component instance is unmounted.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: Optional component instance that receives the hook.

example.title: Clean up a timer
example.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { onBeforeUnmount } from 'vue'

const timer = window.setInterval(() => {
  console.log('tick')
}, 1000)

onBeforeUnmount(() => {
  window.clearInterval(timer)
})
</script>
example.explanation: The hook clears the timer just before the component is removed.

useCases.title: Stop timers
useCases.scenario: A component starts a timer on the client and must stop it before removal.

useCases.title: Release resources
useCases.scenario: A component owns a subscription or external resource that should be released before removal.

interview.question: What does `onBeforeUnmount()` do?
interview.answer: `onBeforeUnmount()` registers a callback that runs right before a component instance is unmounted. The instance is still fully functional when the callback runs.
interview.followUp: Can it be used to clean up browser-only resources during SSR? No. The hook is not called during SSR, so SSR code must not rely on it for cleanup.

interview.question: When would you use this hook?
interview.answer: Use it to perform work that must happen before removal, such as stopping a timer or releasing a resource owned by the component. Register the callback during the component's `setup()` phase.
interview.followUp: When should browser-only setup happen in an SSR app? Put it in `onMounted()`, then clean it up with `onBeforeUnmount()` on the client.

interview.question: What are its callback inputs and return value?
interview.answer: The callback receives no documented arguments and returns nothing. The registration function itself has an optional target component instance parameter, but normal component code usually calls it with only the callback.
interview.followUp: What is the registration signature? `onBeforeUnmount(callback: () => void, target?: ComponentInternalInstance | null): void`.

keyPoints: It registers code that runs immediately before Vue removes the component instance.
The component remains usable inside the callback, so final cleanup can happen before removal.
It runs on the client lifecycle, not while Vue renders on the server.
Its signature takes a no-argument callback and an optional component target, and it returns `void`.
gotchas: Register the hook synchronously during `setup()`; calling it later does not follow the documented usage rule.
Do not depend on this hook for cleanup during SSR. Server-side rendering does not call it.

onMounted.summary: onMounted() registers a callback that runs after a Vue component is mounted. Use it for work that needs the component's rendered DOM, such as reading a template ref or starting a browser-side effect.
onMounted.explanation: Call onMounted during synchronous component setup to register work that should run after the component's DOM exists. Vue invokes the callback after synchronous children mount and the component's DOM is inserted. Use a matching cleanup hook for effects that must stop when the component is removed.
onMounted.syntax: function onMounted(callback: () => void, target?: ComponentInternalInstance | null): void

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: A callback that Vue calls after the component is mounted.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: Optional component instance that receives the hook registration.

example.title: Register and clean up a browser listener
example.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { onMounted, onUnmounted } from 'vue'

function handleResize() {
  console.log(window.innerWidth)
}

onMounted(() => window.addEventListener('resize', handleResize))
onUnmounted(() => window.removeEventListener('resize', handleResize))
</script>
example.explanation: This adds a browser event listener after mount and removes it when the component is destroyed.

useCases.title: Read or modify rendered DOM
useCases.scenario: A template ref points to an input or other rendered element.

useCases.title: Start a client-side effect
useCases.scenario: A component starts a window listener, timer, or external connection.

interview.question: When does onMounted run?
interview.answer: onMounted registers a callback that Vue runs after the component is mounted. At that point, synchronous child components are mounted and the component's DOM has been created and inserted.
interview.followUp: How can you use it with server rendering? onMounted does not run during server-side rendering, so browser-only work belongs there and server data work should use onServerPrefetch when appropriate.

interview.question: Where must onMounted be called?
interview.answer: Register it during synchronous setup, including from a synchronous helper called by setup. Vue uses the current active component instance to associate the callback with the component.
interview.followUp: Why does a delayed registration fail? A timer runs after setup's synchronous call stack has ended, so Vue no longer has the needed active component context.

interview.question: What is a common use for onMounted?
interview.answer: Use onMounted for DOM-dependent side effects, such as reading a template ref or starting a browser listener. Remove manually created listeners, timers, or connections when the component unmounts.
interview.followUp: What should happen if the DOM changes after a reactive update? Use onUpdated for general post-update work, or nextTick when you need the DOM after one specific state change.

keyPoints: onMounted runs after the component finishes mounting.
The hook is a suitable place to access rendered DOM elements.
Synchronous child components are mounted before the parent’s onMounted callback runs.
Use it for DOM-related side effects, such as initializing a browser library.
Vue connects the callback to the active component when setup registers it.
A helper function may register the hook if setup calls that helper synchronously.
gotchas: Register the hook synchronously during setup; calling it later inside a timer does not associate it with the component.
Do not depend on onMounted for server-side work.
Do not depend on onUnmounted for server-side cleanup.

onUnmounted.summary: onUnmounted() registers a callback that runs after a component is unmounted. Use it to clean up manually created side effects such as timers, event listeners, and server connections.
onUnmounted.explanation: Call onUnmounted() to register code that runs after a component is removed. Vue has already unmounted the child components and stopped reactive effects created during setup(), so this hook is useful for cleaning up timers, event listeners, and connections created manually.
onUnmounted.syntax: function onUnmounted(callback: () => void, target?: ComponentInternalInstance | null): void

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: The function Vue calls after the component is unmounted.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: Optional component instance to which the hook is registered.

example.title: Clean up a timer
example.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { onMounted, onUnmounted } from 'vue'

let timer: ReturnType<typeof setInterval>

onMounted(() => {
  timer = setInterval(() => console.log('tick'), 1000)
})

onUnmounted(() => clearInterval(timer))
</script>
example.explanation: Starts a timer after mounting and clears it when the component is removed.
