useCases.scenario: A component starts polling or schedules repeated work.

useCases.title: Remove event listeners
useCases.scenario: A component subscribes to browser events.

useCases.title: Close external resources
useCases.scenario: A component opens a connection or subscription.

interview.question: What does onUnmounted() do?
interview.answer: onUnmounted() registers a callback that runs after the component is unmounted. At that point, child components are unmounted and reactive effects created during setup() have stopped.
interview.followUp: How should a component clean up a manually added event listener? Register removeEventListener() in onUnmounted(), using the same target, event name, and callback.

interview.question: When should you use onUnmounted()?
interview.answer: Use it for manually created side effects, such as timers, DOM event listeners, or server connections. The callback runs after the component has been removed.
interview.followUp: Why is cleanup needed for a timer? Without clearInterval(), the timer can continue running after the component is gone.

interview.question: When must onUnmounted() be called?
interview.answer: The hook must be registered synchronously while setup() is running. Vue uses the current active component instance to associate the callback with that component.
interview.followUp: Can a helper function register the hook? Yes, if the helper is called synchronously from setup() and the hook registration remains synchronous.

keyPoints: The callback runs after unmounting finishes.
Child components are already unmounted when this callback runs.
Vue stops the component's render effect and setup-created computed values and watchers before this hook runs.
Use it to release resources that your code created outside Vue's automatic effect handling.
Lifecycle registration depends on an active component instance during setup.
gotchas: Register the hook synchronously during setup(). Calling it later, such as inside setTimeout(), does not associate it with the component.
Do not depend on this hook for cleanup during server-side rendering.

onUpdated.summary: onUpdated registers a callback that runs after a reactive state change updates a component's DOM. Use nextTick() when you need to wait for one specific state change.
onUpdated.explanation: onUpdated registers a callback that runs after a reactive state change causes the component's DOM tree to update. Vue may combine several state changes into one render cycle, so use nextTick() when the callback must follow one specific change.
onUpdated.syntax: function onUpdated(callback: () => void, target?: ComponentInternalInstance | null): void

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Function called after the component's DOM update.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: Optional component instance whose hook receives the callback.

example.title: Read the DOM after an update
example.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref, onUpdated } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
onUpdated(() => {
  console.log(document.getElementById('count')?.textContent)
})
</script>

<template>
  <button id="count" @click="count++">{{ count }}</button>
</template>
example.explanation: The callback reads the button text after Vue updates the component DOM.

useCases.title: Inspect updated DOM
useCases.scenario: Read or inspect rendered elements after Vue applies an update.

useCases.title: Perform post-update DOM work
useCases.scenario: Run client-side DOM-related work after reactive rendering completes.

interview.question: When does onUpdated run?
interview.answer: onUpdated runs after a reactive state change updates the component's DOM. Multiple changes can be combined into one render cycle.
interview.followUp: How can code wait for one particular state change? Use nextTick() instead of relying on onUpdated.

interview.question: Where should onUpdated be called?
interview.answer: Register onUpdated during the component's synchronous setup phase. Vue connects the callback to the active component instance.
interview.followUp: Can an external helper register it? Yes, if the helper is called synchronously from setup().

interview.question: What is a suitable use for onUpdated?
interview.answer: The hook is useful when code needs to inspect the component DOM after an update. It is not suitable for changing component state.
interview.followUp: What happens if state is changed there? The change can cause an infinite update loop.

keyPoints: onUpdated runs after reactive state changes update the component DOM.
A parent component's hook runs after its child components' hooks.
It can run after any DOM update, not only one named state change.
Vue can batch several state changes into one render cycle.
gotchas: Do not change component state inside the callback. That can trigger repeated updates.
The callback does not run during server-side rendering.
Register the hook synchronously during setup().

Options API.summary: Use defineComponent() for TypeScript inference in Vue Options API components. Use PropType for complex object props and typed callback props.
Options API.explanation: Wrap an Options API component with defineComponent to infer simple prop types. Use PropType when a prop needs a complex object type or a function signature.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Component options containing props, provide, or other Options API options.

Options API.returns: A Vue component definition with inferred Options API types.

example.title: Typed object prop
example.explanation: defineComponent enables prop inference. PropType gives the object its nested TypeScript fields.

useCases.title: Infer prop types
useCases.scenario: A component uses the Options API and needs inferred prop types.

useCases.title: Type object props
useCases.scenario: A prop contains nested object fields.

useCases.title: Type function props
useCases.scenario: A component accepts a callback with typed arguments.

useCases.title: Provide dependencies
useCases.scenario: An ancestor shares values with descendants.

interview.question: How does TypeScript infer Options API prop types?
interview.answer: Use defineComponent() around an Options API component. Vue can then infer prop types from the props option, including required and default settings.
interview.followUp: How do you type a nested object prop? Use PropType<T>, such as Object as PropType<Book>.

interview.question: When should PropType be used?
interview.answer: Use PropType for types that runtime constructors cannot express. It can describe object fields and function parameter and return types.
interview.followUp: What happens without PropType for an object? The runtime Object constructor does not provide the nested property type to TypeScript.

interview.question: How does provide work in the Options API?
interview.answer: provide can be an object or a function returning an object. Descendants can inject those values when they are in the same parent chain.
interview.followUp: Is provided component state reactive by default? No. The documented example says a provided value copied from data is not reactive.

keyPoints: Use defineComponent() to enable TypeScript inference for Options API props.
Required and default prop settings affect the inferred type.
Use PropType when a prop is an object with known fields or a typed callback.
The provide option accepts an object or a function that creates one.
Injected values are available to descendants in the same component parent chain.
gotchas: Runtime prop declarations cannot describe nested object shapes or function call signatures by themselves.
Values returned from provide are not automatically reactive when they come from component state.
Use extends for inheritance, not as a general replacement for composing reusable logic.

provide.summary: provide() makes a value available to descendant components. inject() retrieves it by key, including values provided at app level.
provide.explanation: Use provide() in an ancestor and inject() in a descendant to share a value without passing it through every intermediate component. Vue finds the nearest provider for the key, and injected refs stay refs.
provide.syntax:
provide<T>(key: InjectionKey<T> | string, value: T): void
inject<T>(key: InjectionKey<T> | string, defaultValue?: T): T | undefined
inject<T>(key: InjectionKey<T> | string, defaultValue: () => T, treatDefaultAsFactory: true): T

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The lookup key. It can be a string, Symbol, or typed InjectionKey.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value made available to descendant components.

parameters.name: defaultValue
parameters.description: The value returned when no provider is found.

parameters.name: defaultValue
parameters.description: A factory for the default value; pass true as the third argument.

provide.returns: provide() returns void. inject() returns the provided value, or undefined without a provider or default.

example.title: Provide a reactive value with a typed key
example.explanation: The provider stores a reactive ref under a shared key. A descendant can inject the same ref and update its value.

useCases.title: Avoid prop drilling
useCases.scenario: A deeply nested component needs shared data from an ancestor without passing props through every intermediate component.

useCases.title: Share app-level dependencies
useCases.scenario: A plugin or application-wide service must be available to all rendered components.

useCases.title: Share reactive state and actions
useCases.scenario: A provider owns reactive state and exposes state plus functions that update it.

interview.question: What problem do provide() and inject() solve?
interview.answer: provide() makes a value available to descendant components. inject() looks up that value by key through the ancestor chain. It avoids passing props through components that do not use them.
interview.followUp: What happens when several ancestors use the same key? The provider closest to the injecting component wins and shadows higher providers.

interview.question: Why use Symbol or InjectionKey keys?
interview.answer: The key may be a string or a Symbol. Symbol keys are safer in large applications because unrelated providers are less likely to use the same key. With TypeScript, InjectionKey can connect the value type between provide() and inject().
interview.followUp: How would you share a typed service? Export an InjectionKey<Service> from a shared file, then use that key in both provide() and inject().

interview.question: How does reactivity work with dependency injection?
interview.answer: Provide a ref, reactive object, or computed value when the descendant must stay connected to provider state. A ref is injected as the same ref, so it keeps its reactivity connection. To limit mutations, provide readonly(value).
interview.followUp: How can an injector request an update safely? Provide a function that performs the mutation in the provider, and expose that function with the state.

keyPoints: provide() takes a key and a value. The key identifies the dependency.
inject() searches ancestor components for a matching key.
If several ancestors provide the key, the nearest provider supplies the value.
app.provide() makes a dependency available throughout the application.
A provided value may be any type, including a ref or other reactive state.
inject() accepts an optional default value when a provider may be absent.
gotchas: Call provide() synchronously during setup(). The same rule applies to inject().
Without a provider or default, inject() can return undefined.
An injected ref is not unwrapped. Use its .value in JavaScript.
An Options API provide() function does not make ordinary values reactive. Provide a ref or computed value when reactivity is needed.

reactive.summary: reactive() returns a deeply reactive Proxy for an object. Use the proxy to read and change state so Vue can track those changes.
reactive.explanation: reactive() returns a Proxy that tracks reads and writes on an object. The conversion is deep, so nested objects also become reactive. Use the returned proxy for state access; changing the original object does not trigger updates.
reactive.syntax: function reactive<T extends object>(target: T): UnwrapNestedRefs<T>

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The object to convert into a reactive proxy. It must be an object type, such as an object, array, Map, or Set.

reactive.returns: A deeply reactive proxy with nested refs unwrapped where supported. The proxy is not equal to the original object.

example.title: Create a reactive object
example.code:
import { reactive } from 'vue'

const state = reactive({ count: 0 })
state.count++
console.log(state.count) // 1
example.explanation: This creates a reactive object and changes one of its properties.

useCases.title: Reactive state object
useCases.scenario: Manage component state with several related properties.

useCases.title: Deep state updates
useCases.scenario: Track changes inside nested objects or arrays.

useCases.title: Reactive collections
useCases.scenario: Use a Map or Set as reactive application state.

interview.question: What does reactive() return?
interview.answer: reactive() takes an object and returns a reactive Proxy. Vue tracks property access and changes, including nested properties because conversion is deep.
interview.followUp: What happens if the original object is changed? Changes to the original object do not trigger updates; use the returned proxy instead.

interview.question: How does the reactive proxy relate to the original object?
interview.answer: The returned proxy is not equal to the original object. Calling reactive() again with the same object returns the same proxy, and passing the proxy to reactive() returns that proxy.
interview.followUp: Why should code use the proxy? Only the proxy is reactive, so state should be accessed and changed through it.

interview.question: What are the main limitations of reactive()?
interview.answer: reactive() is limited to objects, arrays, and collections such as Map and Set. It cannot hold primitive values, cannot replace the whole reactive object safely, and loses reactivity when primitive properties are destructured.
interview.followUp: What API is recommended when these limits are a problem? Use ref() as the primary API for declaring reactive state.

keyPoints: reactive() wraps an object in a reactive Proxy.
Nested objects are also made reactive when accessed.
Refs used as properties of a deep reactive object are automatically unwrapped.
Refs inside reactive arrays or collections still need .value.
Repeated calls with the same raw object return the same proxy.
gotchas: The returned proxy is not the same object as the original. Do not use the original object as your reactive state.
Replacing the whole reactive object breaks the tracking connection. Keep the same reactive object and change its properties.
Destructuring a primitive property disconnects the local variable from the reactive object.

Reactivity system.summary: ref() creates a reactive, mutable container with a .value property. Vue tracks reads and triggers effects when that value changes.
Reactivity system.explanation: A ref stores a value in an object with a .value property. Vue tracks reads of .value and runs connected effects when the value changes. If the value is an object, ref() makes that object deeply reactive; use shallowRef() to avoid that conversion.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The initial value stored in the ref. It may be a primitive or an object.

Reactivity system.returns: A Ref<UnwrapRef<T>> object with a mutable, reactive .value property.

example.title: Create and update a ref
example.explanation: This creates a number ref, changes its value through .value, and reads the updated value.

useCases.title: Store a reactive value
useCases.scenario: A counter, loading flag, selected ID, or other single value must update the Vue UI.

useCases.title: Share reactive state with functions
useCases.scenario: A value must move into a composable or helper while keeping its live reactivity.

useCases.title: Wrap reactive object state
useCases.scenario: An object should be reactive but should still be accessed through a stable ref interface.

interview.question: What does ref() return, and how does Vue track it?
interview.answer: ref() returns a mutable object with one .value property. Vue tracks reads from .value and triggers effects after writes to it. Object values are deeply converted to reactive state.
interview.followUp: How can deep conversion be avoided? Use shallowRef(), which keeps the inner value unchanged and tracks only the ref's .value.

interview.question: When should reactive() be used?
interview.answer: reactive() returns a Proxy for an object, array, Map, or Set. The proxy tracks property access and updates caused by property changes. It cannot directly represent primitive values.
interview.followUp: Why can replacing a reactive object be a problem? Tracking is tied to the original object reference, so assigning a new reactive object loses that connection.

interview.question: Why does Vue use .value for refs?
interview.answer: Plain local variables cannot be intercepted when JavaScript reads or changes them. A ref uses .value so Vue can intercept the property's getter and setter for dependency tracking and triggering.
interview.followUp: Why are refs useful when extracting reusable logic? Passing a ref preserves access to the latest value and keeps its reactivity connection.

keyPoints: ref() wraps a value in a reactive, mutable object.
Read or write the stored value through the .value property.
Vue records effects that read a ref and reruns them when the ref changes.
Object values inside a ref become deeply reactive, including nested objects.
Use shallowRef() when only changes to the outer .value should be reactive.
A ref can be passed to another function without losing its current value or reactivity.
gotchas: reactive() cannot be used to store a primitive value. Use ref() for strings, numbers, booleans, and other single values.
After reactive() returns a proxy, update the proxy rather than the original object.
Destructuring a primitive property from a reactive object disconnects that local variable from the original reactive state.

readonly.summary: `readonly()` returns a readonly proxy for an object or ref. Reads remain reactive, but writes through the proxy are blocked and warn.
readonly.explanation: `readonly()` wraps an object or ref in a deep readonly proxy. Reading it still participates in reactivity, but changing it through the proxy is blocked and produces a warning.
readonly.syntax: function readonly<T extends object>(target: T): DeepReadonly<UnwrapNestedRefs<T>>

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The plain object, reactive object, or ref to wrap.

readonly.returns: A deep readonly proxy around the target, with nested properties also readonly.

example.title: Create a readonly proxy
example.explanation: The readonly proxy still tracks changes from the original object, but writes through the proxy are blocked.

useCases.title: Protect shared state
useCases.scenario: Expose state to code that should read but not modify it.

useCases.title: Read-only reactive views
useCases.scenario: Let effects observe source changes without giving them write access.

useCases.title: Protect nested data
useCases.scenario: Make nested configuration values immutable through the exposed proxy.

interview.question: What does `readonly()` return?
interview.answer: `readonly()` accepts an object or ref and returns a readonly proxy to the original value. The proxy prevents writes while preserving reactive tracking.
interview.followUp: What happens when the source object changes? A watcher using the readonly proxy can still react to those source changes.

interview.question: Is the readonly conversion shallow or deep?
interview.answer: The conversion is deep. Nested properties reached through the proxy are readonly too.
interview.followUp: How can you limit readonly behavior to the root? Use `shallowReadonly()`, which does not convert nested values.

interview.question: How does `readonly()` handle refs?
interview.answer: A readonly proxy follows the ref-unwrapping behavior of `reactive()`. Unlike `reactive()`, the values exposed after unwrapping are also made readonly.
interview.followUp: Why might `shallowReadonly()` be useful? It keeps property values as-is and does not automatically unwrap ref values.

keyPoints: It accepts a plain object, reactive object, or ref.
Nested values become readonly when accessed through the proxy.
Writing through the readonly proxy does not change the value and causes a warning.
Watchers can track the readonly proxy and respond when the original changes.
gotchas: Readonly behavior also applies to nested properties.
Use `shallowReadonly()` when only root-level properties should be readonly.

ref.summary: `isRef()` checks whether a value is a ref. `unref()` reads a ref's inner value or returns a plain value unchanged.
ref.explanation: `isRef()` checks whether a value is a ref object. Its result narrows the type for TypeScript. `unref()` returns `.value` for a ref, but returns other values unchanged. Use `unref()` when code accepts either a plain value or a ref.
ref.syntax:
function isRef<T>(r: Ref<T> | unknown): r is Ref<T>
function unref<T>(ref: T | Ref<T>): T

parameters.name: r / ref
parameters.type: Ref<T> | unknown for isRef(); T | Ref<T> for unref()
parameters.description: Value to test or unwrap.

ref.returns: `isRef()` returns a boolean type predicate. `unref()` returns the inner value or the original non-ref value.

example.title: Check and read a ref
example.code:
import { ref, isRef, unref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(1)

console.log(isRef(count)) // true
console.log(unref(count)) // 1
console.log(unref('ready')) // 'ready'
example.explanation: This checks whether `count` is a ref and reads its inner value. `unref()` leaves a non-ref value unchanged.

useCases.title: Narrow an unknown value
useCases.scenario: A function accepts an unknown input and needs to safely use `.value` only for refs.

useCases.title: Normalize a value
useCases.scenario: A composable accepts either a plain value or a ref and needs one usable value.

interview.question: What does `isRef()` do?
interview.answer: `isRef()` tests whether a value is a ref object. It returns a boolean and can narrow an unknown value to `Ref<unknown>` in TypeScript.
interview.followUp: How would you read the value without checking first? Use `unref()`, which returns the inner value for refs and returns non-ref inputs unchanged.

interview.question: When should you use `unref()`?
interview.answer: `unref()` accepts either a value or a ref. It is equivalent to checking with `isRef()` and then reading `.value` when needed.
interview.followUp: Does `unref()` evaluate getters? No. Getter support is provided by `toValue()`, not `unref()`.

interview.question: How are `isRef()` and `unref()` different?
interview.answer: `isRef()` is useful when the code must branch on ref behavior or needs TypeScript narrowing. `unref()` is useful when the code only needs the current value.
interview.followUp: What utility also handles getters? `toValue()` normalizes plain values, refs, and getters to values.

keyPoints: `isRef(value)` tells you whether `value` is a ref.
The TypeScript type guard narrows an unknown value to a ref after a successful check.
`unref(value)` unwraps a ref and leaves a plain value as it is.
`unref()` is shorthand for a conditional ref check followed by reading `.value`.
gotchas: In TypeScript, `isRef()` is also a type guard, so a successful check narrows the value to a ref.

parameters.name: exactActiveClass
parameters.description: Class applied when the link is exactly active.

<template>

</template>

<style>
.router-link-active { color: blue; }
.router-link-exact-active { font-weight: bold; }
</style>

useCases.title: Nested route styling

interview.question: When does Vue Router consider a RouterLink active?
interview.answer: A link is active when it matches the current route record and has the same parameter values. A nested ancestor link can also be active when its relevant parameters match.
interview.followUp: What route data is ignored? Query values are ignored, and redirects are not followed for this check.

interview.question: What is the difference between active and exact-active classes?
interview.answer: router-link-active includes matching ancestor routes. router-link-exact-active requires an exact match and does not include ancestor routes.
interview.followUp: How would you make a parent link active for child pages? Nest the child routes under the parent route.

interview.question: How can active-link class names be customized?
interview.answer: Use activeClass and exactActiveClass on an individual RouterLink. Set linkActiveClass and linkExactActiveClass in createRouter to change the defaults globally.
interview.followUp: How can a custom component inspect active state? Use RouterLink with v-slot, or use the useLink Composition API function.

keyPoints: Active status uses the configured route record, not only the visible URL path.
Route parameters must have the same values as the current location.
In nested routes, a matching ancestor link can receive the active class.
The exact-active state excludes parent or ancestor route matches.
RouterLink provides separate CSS classes for active and exact-active states.
Per-link class names can be changed with activeClass and exactActiveClass.
gotchas: Query parameters do not decide whether a RouterLink is active.
A redirect is not followed during active-link checking.
Two routes with the same path are not necessarily related; their route records must match.

RouterView.summary: RouterView renders the component matched by the current route. Its slot lets you wrap that component with features such as KeepAlive or Transition.
RouterView.explanation: RouterView is the component that renders the component matched by the current route. Its slot exposes that matched component so you can wrap it with features such as KeepAlive or Transition.

parameters.name: Component
parameters.description: The component instance used by the RouterView slot.

parameters.name: route
parameters.description: The normalized route location associated with the rendered view.

RouterView.returns: A VNode array representing the rendered route view.

example.code:
<router-view v-slot="{ Component }">

    <component :is="Component" />
  </keep-alive>
</router-view>
example.explanation: This renders the active route component and keeps its state alive when the user changes routes.

useCases.scenario: Keep route components mounted across navigation.

useCases.title: Add route transitions
useCases.scenario: Animate the component shown when the route changes.

useCases.title: Customize route rendering

interview.question: What does RouterView do?
interview.answer: RouterView renders the component selected by the current route. Without a slot, it handles that rendering directly; with a slot, it exposes the component for custom rendering.
interview.followUp: How can route components be kept alive? Place KeepAlive inside the RouterView slot around the dynamic component.

interview.question: How do you render a RouterView slot?
interview.answer: The slot provides a Component value. Render it with the Vue component element's is binding, such as <component :is="Component" />.
interview.followUp: Why use the slot instead of only RouterView? It lets you add wrappers such as KeepAlive and Transition around the route component.

interview.question: How do RouterView, KeepAlive, and Transition work together?
interview.answer: KeepAlive should wrap the route component inside the RouterView slot. Transition can also wrap the route component, and KeepAlive can be placed inside that Transition.
interview.followUp: What limitation applies when passing props through the slot? All route components used there need compatible props and slots.

keyPoints: RouterView displays the component for the user's current route.
Its slot gives control over how the active route component is rendered.
Rendering the exposed component normally has the same basic result as using RouterView without a slot.
Use the slot to animate changes between route components.
The slot can provide extra props or slot content to the selected route component.
gotchas: Put KeepAlive inside the RouterView slot so it preserves route components rather than the RouterView wrapper.
Passing props or slots through RouterView can require every route component to support the same interface.

Scoped CSS.summary: Scoped CSS limits component styles by compiling selectors with a unique attribute. It also supports global styles in the same component and deep selectors for reaching child components.
Scoped CSS.explanation: Vue Loader rewrites selectors in a scoped style and adds a matching unique attribute to elements in the component. This keeps normal selectors local. A child component root can still receive the parent's scoped styles, which supports layout styling. Use a deep selector when a rule must reach deeper into a child component.

example.title: A scoped component style
example.code:
<style scoped>
.button { color: red; }
</style>

<template>
  <button class="button">Save</button>
</template>
example.explanation: The style applies to this component's button because Vue adds a matching unique attribute to the selector and element.

useCases.title: Component-local styling
useCases.scenario: Keep a component's visual rules from affecting unrelated components.

useCases.title: Mixed style scope
useCases.scenario: Add a global reset and local component rules in one single-file component.

useCases.title: Deep child styling
useCases.scenario: Style an element inside a child component when normal scoped matching stops at the boundary.

interview.question: How does scoped CSS work?
interview.answer: The scoped attribute tells Vue Loader to limit the style to the current component. It rewrites selectors and adds a matching unique attribute to component elements.
interview.followUp: How can a parent style content inside a child component? Use a deep selector such as >>>, /deep/, or ::v-deep.

interview.question: What happens at a child component boundary?
interview.answer: A parent scoped rule does not normally reach into a child component. The child component's root element is an exception and can match both components' scoped rules.
interview.followUp: Why allow the exception? It lets the parent control layout of the child component root.

interview.question: Can local and global styles coexist?
interview.answer: A component can contain both ordinary and scoped style blocks. Ordinary styles remain global, while the block with scoped limits its rules to the component.
interview.followUp: What should be used when preprocessing cannot parse >>>? Use /deep/ or ::v-deep, which the documentation describes as aliases.

keyPoints: A scoped style is intended to affect elements owned by the current component.
Vue Loader uses PostCSS to transform scoped CSS during compilation.
The compiled selector receives a unique data attribute, such as data-v-f3f3eg9.
One component may use both global style blocks and local scoped style blocks.
Use >>> when a scoped selector must affect a descendant component.
/deep/ and ::v-deep provide alternative spelling for the deep selector.
gotchas: Some preprocessors may reject the >>> combinator. Use /deep/ or ::v-deep instead; these are aliases with the same behavior.
A child component root is affected by both parent and child scoped styles. Do not assume that scoped styles exclude that root element.

script setup.summary: <script setup> is Vue's concise syntax for using the Composition API in Single-File Components. Top-level code is available to the template, and compiler macros declare props, events, models, and other component features.
script setup.explanation: The compiler turns the contents of <script setup> into a component's setup function. Top-level imports, variables, and functions become available in the template, while compiler macros declare component features such as props, events, exposed members, and options.

parameters.name: props declaration
parameters.type: runtime object, array, or type argument
parameters.description: Optional runtime options or a literal type describing component props.

parameters.name: emits declaration
parameters.description: Optional runtime options or a type describing emitted event names and arguments.

example.title: A basic script setup component
example.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
function increment() {
  count.value++
}
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="increment">Count: {{ count }}</button>
</template>
example.explanation: The component creates reactive state with ref. The template can use the top-level ref and unwrap it automatically.

useCases.title: Write component logic with less boilerplate
useCases.scenario: Authoring Vue Single-File Components with the Composition API

useCases.title: Use top-level bindings in templates
useCases.scenario: Making state, handlers, and imports available to a template

useCases.title: Define a component interface
useCases.scenario: Declaring typed props and emitted events

useCases.title: Control instance exposure
useCases.scenario: Exposing a selected public API to parent refs

interview.question: What is <script setup>?
interview.answer: <script setup> is compile-time syntax for using the Composition API in a Vue Single-File Component. Its contents run when each component instance is created, unlike a normal script that runs once when imported.
interview.followUp: How do top-level declarations reach the template? The compiler exposes top-level imports, variables, and functions directly to template expressions.

interview.question: How are props and emitted events declared?
interview.answer: defineProps and defineEmits are compiler macros available only inside <script setup>. They need no import and are removed during compilation; each accepts either runtime options or a type declaration.
interview.followUp: Can both forms be used together? No. A declaration must use runtime options or types, not both.

interview.question: What changed for destructured props and defaults?
interview.answer: In Vue 3.5 and later, destructured values from defineProps stay reactive because the compiler rewrites accesses to use props.<name>. In Vue 3.4 and earlier, withDefaults supports defaults for type-based props when reactive destructuring is not enabled by default.
interview.followUp: What should a mutable default look like with withDefaults? Use a factory function for arrays or objects so each component instance gets its own value.

keyPoints: It is the recommended concise syntax for Composition API in Vue SFCs.
Instance-specific setup code runs for every new component instance.
Top-level declarations need no separate return or registration step.
Use APIs such as ref to create reactive state; refs are automatically unwrapped in templates.
Imported components can be rendered directly with PascalCase tags.
A local directive is available when its variable follows the vNameOfDirective naming pattern.
These macros declare props and events without imports and disappear during compilation.
Use defineExpose to choose which bindings a parent can access through a template ref.
gotchas: Options passed to defineProps or defineEmits cannot use local variables from setup scope. They may use imported bindings.
Bindings inside script setup are not public through template refs or parent chains unless defineExpose is used.
A default value for defineModel can make the child model differ from an undefined parent ref.
Type-based props and emits are analyzed from syntax, so some complex whole-object types cannot be converted to runtime options.

shallowRef.summary: shallowRef creates a ref that tracks only its .value property. Its inner value is not made deeply reactive, so nested mutations do not trigger effects.
shallowRef.explanation: shallowRef stores its inner value without making nested data reactive. Vue tracks reads and writes of the ref's .value property, so changing a nested property does not trigger effects, but assigning a new value does.
shallowRef.syntax:
function shallowRef<T>(value: T): ShallowRef<T>
interface ShallowRef<T> { value: T }

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value stored in the shallow ref. Nested parts remain unchanged and are not deeply converted.

shallowRef.returns: A ShallowRef<T> with a mutable .value property. The inner value is exposed without deep conversion.

example.title: A shallow reactive reference
example.explanation: Use shallowRef when only replacing the top-level value should trigger reactivity.

useCases.title: Reduce reactivity overhead
useCases.scenario: A large object or array should not be made fully reactive.

useCases.title: Connect external state
useCases.scenario: State is owned or updated by a library outside Vue.

interview.question: How does shallowRef differ from ref?
interview.answer: shallowRef returns a ref whose inner value stays as-is. Vue tracks access to .value, but it does not deeply convert the stored value.
interview.followUp: When should it be used? It is useful for large data structures or when connecting Vue to an external state management system.

interview.question: What changes trigger effects for a shallowRef?
interview.answer: Assigning a new object to .value triggers effects because the top-level ref value is reactive. Mutating a nested property does not trigger them because the inner object is not deeply reactive.
interview.followUp: How can a deep mutation still notify effects? Call triggerRef after changing the nested data.

interview.question: When would you use triggerRef?
interview.answer: triggerRef forces effects that depend on a shallow ref to run. It is useful after making a deep mutation to the value stored inside the shallow ref.
interview.followUp: What limitation remains? The nested data is still not deeply reactive; triggerRef only causes dependent effects to run at that point.

keyPoints: shallowRef creates a top-level reactive ref without deep reactivity for its stored value.
It can reduce reactivity work for large data structures.
It is also suited to values managed by another state system.
Effects depend on reading the ref's .value property.
gotchas: Nested objects are not converted to reactive objects. Deep changes alone do not trigger updates.
Replacing the ref's value triggers reactivity, while changing a property inside that value does not.

Single-file components.summary: A Vue Single-File Component is a .vue file that keeps a component's template, logic, and styles together. A build step processes it and enables features such as scoped CSS, precompiled templates, and hot-module replacement.
Single-file components.explanation: A Single-File Component is a .vue file that keeps a component's template, JavaScript, and CSS together. A build tool processes these blocks, enabling features such as precompiled templates, scoped styles, Composition API syntax, type checking, and hot-module replacement.

example.title: A Vue Single-File Component
example.code:
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
const count = ref(0)
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="count++">Count: {{ count }}</button>
</template>

<style scoped>
button { font-weight: bold; }
</style>
example.explanation: This component keeps its state, markup, and CSS in one .vue file.

useCases.title: Application components
useCases.scenario: Building a full Vue application with a build setup.

useCases.title: Cohesive component files
useCases.scenario: Keeping a component's markup, code, and CSS easy to find.

useCases.title: Composition API development
useCases.scenario: Using Composition API syntax with editor and build-time support.

interview.question: What is a Vue Single-File Component?
interview.answer: A Vue SFC is a .vue file that contains a component's template, script, and style. The format places the view, logic, and styling together, while build tools compile it for use in the application.
interview.followUp: Why can this be better than three large global layers? Components keep closely related concerns together, so each unit is more cohesive and easier to maintain.

interview.question: What do the blocks in an SFC do?
interview.answer: The main blocks are <template>, <script>, and <style>. The template describes the markup, the script contains component logic, and the style contains CSS; a script setup block is also shown for Composition API code.
interview.followUp: What does scoped styling change? In the documented example, <style scoped> limits the component's CSS so its button rules do not act as ordinary global styles.

interview.question: Why use SFCs?
interview.answer: SFCs require a build step, but they provide precompiled templates, component-scoped CSS, more convenient Composition API syntax, compile-time analysis, IDE support, and hot-module replacement. They also colocate related component concerns.
interview.followUp: Which style does the Vue guide recommend for full applications? Composition API with SFCs; Options API is recommended when build tools are not used or the scenario is low complexity.

keyPoints: An SFC is a special .vue file that packages a component's template, logic, and styles.
The main blocks are <template>, <script>, and <style>; they keep the component's view, code, and CSS together.
Build tools precompile the template, so the browser does not need to compile that template at runtime.
A style block can use the scoped attribute to keep CSS rules local to the component.
The SFC format provides convenient syntax for Composition API code, including <script setup>.
SFC projects can provide editor completion and type checking for expressions used in templates.
gotchas: SFC files need a build step, so they are not the usual choice for a small page that only enhances existing HTML.
The exact rules for SFC blocks come from the SFC Syntax Specification; this page gives the main structure rather than every syntax rule.

Slots.summary: Slots let a parent pass template content into a child component. The child renders it with a slot outlet and can support fallback content, named slots, and slot props.
Slots.explanation: Slots let a parent pass template content into a child component. The child places that content with a slot outlet, and can provide fallback content, named outlets, or slot props.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The slot name identifies the child outlet to receive the content. An unnamed outlet uses the name default.

parameters.name: slot props
parameters.description: Slot props are values supplied by the child on the slot outlet and received by the parent.

Slots.returns: Rendered template content at the matching slot outlet.

example.title: Vue component example
example.code:
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="count++">{{ count }}</button>
</template>
example.explanation: This example uses Vue's script setup and a template, but it does not demonstrate slots.

useCases.title: Reusable component content
useCases.scenario: A reusable button or layout owns the outer markup while callers provide its inner content.

useCases.title: Page layouts with named slots
useCases.scenario: A layout places separate parent-provided fragments in header, main, and footer areas.

useCases.title: Flexible list rendering
useCases.scenario: A list supplies each item to a parent-defined template through slot props.

useCases.title: Renderless logic components
useCases.scenario: A component exposes state or behavior while the consumer supplies all visible markup.

interview.question: What is a Vue slot?
interview.answer: A slot lets a parent pass template content to a child. The child renders it where a <slot> outlet appears.
interview.followUp: How can a child provide default content? Put the default content inside the slot outlet; Vue uses it when the parent passes no content.

interview.question: How do named slots work?
interview.answer: Use a name attribute on the child slot outlet, such as <slot name="header">. The parent targets it with <template #header>.
interview.followUp: What happens to top-level non-template children when named slots are used? They are treated as content for the default slot.

interview.question: What are scoped slots?
interview.answer: A child passes values with attributes on the slot outlet, such as <slot :item="item" />. The parent receives them with v-slot, for example <template #item="{ item }">.
interview.followUp: Why are scoped slots useful? They let the child control data or iteration while the parent controls the rendered item template.

keyPoints: Place <slot> in the child template where parent content should appear.
A slot can contain elements, components, and other valid template content.
Use v-slot:name or the shorter #name syntax to target a named slot.
Build slot names dynamically with v-slot:[dynamicSlotName] or #[dynamicSlotName].
A child can pass slot props, and the parent reads them through v-slot variables or destructuring.
gotchas: An unnamed slot is the default slot. Use an explicit name for other outlets.
Vue custom elements support native slot syntax, but they do not support scoped slots.

storeToRefs.summary: storeToRefs() returns refs for a Pinia store’s reactive state and getters. It also includes reactive plugin state, but skips actions and non-reactive properties.
storeToRefs.explanation: Call storeToRefs() with a Pinia store to get refs for its reactive state and getters. It also includes reactive state added by plugins, while leaving out actions and non-reactive properties.

parameters.name: store
parameters.description: The Pinia store from which to extract refs.

storeToRefs.returns: An object containing refs for the store's state, getters, and plugin-added reactive state properties.

example.title: Keep destructured store values reactive
example.code:
import { storeToRefs } from 'pinia'
import { useCounterStore } from '@/stores/counter'

const store = useCounterStore()
const { name, doubleCount } = storeToRefs(store)
const { increment } = store

console.log(name.value, doubleCount.value)
increment()
example.explanation: Use storeToRefs() for reactive store values. Destructure actions directly from the store.

useCases.title: Reactive destructuring
useCases.scenario: Destructure state or getters in a component while keeping updates reactive.

useCases.title: Read-only store data
useCases.scenario: Read store data without extracting actions.

useCases.title: Plugin state
useCases.scenario: Use reactive properties supplied by a Pinia plugin.

interview.question: Why use storeToRefs() instead of destructuring a Pinia store directly?
interview.answer: storeToRefs() creates refs for the store's reactive state and getters. This lets destructured values keep their reactivity.
interview.followUp: What does it exclude? It skips actions and non-reactive properties.

interview.question: How do you call storeToRefs()?
interview.answer: Pass the store instance to storeToRefs(). The result contains refs for reactive store properties.
interview.followUp: How should an action be extracted? Destructure it directly from the store because actions are bound to the store.

interview.question: Does storeToRefs() include state added by plugins?
interview.answer: Plugin-added reactive state is also included in the returned refs. This makes plugin state available when destructuring.
interview.followUp: What kind of plugin property is skipped? A non-reactive plugin property is skipped like any other non-reactive property.

keyPoints: The returned object has refs for store state, getters, and reactive state added by plugins.
It provides a Pinia-specific way to preserve reactivity during destructuring.
Each reactive store property is represented by a ref in the result.
It fits components that read store data without needing to extract actions.
gotchas: Actions and other non-reactive properties are not returned by storeToRefs(). Destructure actions from the store itself.

Suspense.summary: Suspense coordinates nested async dependencies in Vue. It shows fallback content while async setup() components or suspensible async components resolve.
Suspense.explanation: Suspense renders its default slot in memory first. If it finds async setup() components or suspensible async components, it shows the fallback slot until all of them resolve. After resolution, it displays the default content. A timeout can control when fallback content appears after the default root changes.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in milliseconds before fallback content is shown after default content is replaced.

parameters.name: suspensible
parameters.description: Passes async dependency handling to a parent Suspense boundary.

example.title: Show a fallback for async content
example.code:
<Suspense>
  <Dashboard />
  <template #fallback>Loading...</template>
</Suspense>
example.explanation: Vue renders the fallback while Dashboard or its nested async dependencies finish.

useCases.title: Show one page-level loading state
useCases.scenario: A page contains several nested components that load data asynchronously.

useCases.title: Keep old content while new content loads
useCases.scenario: A route switches to a component with new async dependencies.

useCases.title: Coordinate nested loading boundaries
useCases.scenario: Several async boundaries exist in nested layouts or routes.

interview.question: What problem does Suspense solve?
interview.answer: Suspense coordinates async setup() components and suspensible async components. It renders the default slot in memory, then shows the fallback if unresolved dependencies exist.
interview.followUp: How does an async component avoid Suspense control? Set suspensible: false so the component manages its own loading, error, delay, and timeout behavior.

interview.question: How does Suspense choose between default and fallback content?
interview.answer: On the first render, Suspense tries the default slot. If async dependencies are found, it enters pending state and displays the fallback. After all dependencies resolve, it displays the default slot.
interview.followUp: What happens when deeper async content changes after resolution? It does not re-enter pending unless the default slot's root node is replaced.

interview.question: Which props and events does Suspense provide?
interview.answer: Suspense has timeout, suspensible, and the resolve, pending, and fallback events. The timeout is measured in milliseconds and controls when fallback appears after new default content replaces the old content.
interview.followUp: What value shows fallback immediately after replacement? A timeout of 0 makes fallback content appear immediately.

keyPoints: It coordinates async work across nested components and can provide one top-level loading state.
Components with async setup() are dependencies that Suspense waits for.
Async components normally participate in a parent Suspense boundary.
The default slot appears after every dependency found during rendering resolves.
Use the fallback event to react when loading content becomes visible.
Nested Suspense boundaries are supported starting in Vue 3.3.
gotchas: Suspense is experimental, so its API may change.
Each slot accepts only one immediate child node.
Handle async errors with errorCaptured or onErrorCaptured in a parent component.

Teleport.summary: Teleport renders part of a component's template in another DOM location. The component's logical relationships remain unchanged.
Teleport.explanation: Teleport moves template content to a DOM target outside its original DOM location. The component relationships, props, events, and dependency injection still follow the original component tree.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: Required CSS selector or DOM element where the slot content is rendered.

parameters.name: disabled
parameters.description: Keeps content in its original location when true. It can change dynamically.

parameters.name: defer
parameters.description: Defers target resolution until other application parts mount. Available in Vue 3.5+.

Teleport.returns: A component that renders its slot content in the target DOM container.

example.title: Teleport a modal to the document body
example.explanation: The modal stays in this component's logical tree but its rendered HTML is placed under the document body.

useCases.title: Render overlays outside nested layout elements
useCases.scenario: A modal, dialog, or overlay needs to escape ancestor CSS positioning and stacking contexts.

useCases.title: Switch between teleported and inline content
useCases.scenario: The same component should appear inline on small screens and as an overlay on larger screens.

useCases.title: Append multiple overlays to one target
useCases.scenario: Several reusable modal instances need one shared container.

interview.question: What does Teleport change?
interview.answer: Teleport moves rendered content to another DOM node. It does not move the component in Vue's logical tree, so props, emitted events, and injections continue to work normally.
interview.followUp: What happens to the child in Vue Devtools? It remains under its original parent component, even though its HTML appears elsewhere in the DOM.

interview.question: What can the `to` prop point to?
interview.answer: The `to` prop accepts a CSS selector string or an actual DOM element. The selected target must be present when Teleport resolves it.
interview.followUp: How can a target rendered later by Vue be used? In Vue 3.5 or later, use `defer`, but render the target in the same mount or update tick.

interview.question: How can Teleport be disabled?
interview.answer: Set `disabled` to true to keep the content at its original location. This can be changed dynamically, for example to switch between an overlay and inline content.
interview.followUp: Can multiple Teleports use one target? Yes. Vue appends later mounts after earlier content in that target.

keyPoints: Teleport is built into Vue, so it can be used directly in a template without registration.
Use `to` with a CSS selector or an actual DOM node.
Only the rendered DOM location changes. The logical component hierarchy stays the same.
Props and emitted events work normally across the teleported boundary.
A teleported child can still receive injected values from its parent.
Use `disabled` to conditionally keep content in its original DOM location.
In Vue 3.5 and later, `defer` delays target resolution until other application parts have mounted.
gotchas: The target must exist before Teleport mounts. Use a target outside the Vue app when possible.
Several Teleports can share one target. Their content is appended in mount order.
With defer, the target cannot appear a later second. It must be available in the same mount or update tick.

toRef.summary: toRef() turns a value, ref, or getter into a ref, or links a ref to a property on a reactive object. The linked ref and source property stay synchronized.
toRef.explanation: toRef() creates a ref for a property on a reactive object. Changes through the ref update the source property, and changes to the source update the ref. In Vue 3.3 and later, it can also normalize a value, an existing ref, or a getter into a ref.
toRef.syntax:
function toRef<T>(value: T): T extends () => infer R ? Readonly<Ref<R>> : T extends Ref ? T : Ref<UnwrapRef<T>>
function toRef<T extends object, K extends keyof T>(object: T, key: K, defaultValue?: T[K]): ToRef<T[K]>

parameters.name: object
parameters.description: The source object containing the property.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The property name or key to link.

parameters.name: defaultValue
parameters.description: The value to use when the property is missing.

toRef.returns: A ref linked to the selected property. In the normalization form, it may return the existing ref, a writable ref for a value, or a read-only ref for a getter.

example.title: Create a linked property ref
example.code:
import { reactive, toRef } from 'vue'

const state = reactive({ count: 1 })
const count = toRef(state, 'count')

count.value++
console.log(state.count) // 2

state.count++
console.log(count.value) // 3
example.explanation: The ref and the reactive object's property stay linked in both directions.

useCases.title: Pass a prop to a composable
useCases.scenario: A composable needs one component prop as a ref.

useCases.title: Keep a property linked
useCases.scenario: A reactive object's property must be exposed as a ref.

useCases.title: Normalize an input
useCases.scenario: A composable accepts values, refs, or getters through one API.

toRef.since: 3.3+ for the normalization signature; the page does not stat

interview.question: What does the object-property form of toRef do?
interview.answer: toRef(state, 'foo') returns a ref linked to state.foo. Updating either one updates the other.
interview.followUp: Why does ref(state.foo) behave differently? It receives the current plain value, so it is not linked to state.foo.

interview.question: What inputs can the normalization form accept?
interview.answer: In Vue 3.3 and later, toRef(value) accepts a value, an existing ref, or a getter. A value becomes a normal ref, an existing ref is returned as-is, and a getter becomes a read-only ref.
interview.followUp: When might a getter be useful? It lets a composable accept reactive access such as toRef(() => props.foo) without first creating an intermediate computed ref.

interview.question: How does toRef differ from toRefs?
interview.answer: toRef(state, 'foo') is for one property. toRefs(state) converts the enumerable properties present at the call time into linked refs, which is useful when returning reactive state from a composable.
interview.followUp: What should be used for a property that does not exist yet? Use toRef for that property, because toRefs only handles properties enumerable at call time.

keyPoints: Use toRef(object, key) when a composable needs one property as a ref.
The returned ref provides two-way synchronization with the source property.
With the normalization form, passing an existing ref returns that same ref instead of creating another one.
Passing a getter creates a read-only ref whose value is obtained when .value is read.
Passing a non-function value creates a standard ref.
Use toRef to pass a prop as a ref to a composable while retaining its reactive connection.
gotchas: Do not use ref(state.foo) when you need a linked ref. That creates a ref from the current value only, so later changes are not synchronized.
A ref made from a component prop does not remove Vue's normal prop mutation restrictions.
For a property that may be added later, use toRef instead of toRefs.

toRefs.summary: toRefs converts a reactive object into an object of linked refs. This lets you destructure returned state without losing reactivity.
toRefs.explanation: toRefs converts every property of a reactive object into a ref linked to that property. Changes through either the original object or a returned ref are visible through the other side. This lets a composable return state that callers can destructure without losing reactivity.
toRefs.syntax: function toRefs<T extends object>(object: T): { [K in keyof T]: ToRef<T[K]> }

parameters.name: object
parameters.description: A reactive object whose properties should become linked refs.

toRefs.returns: An object with the same keys, where each property is a ref linked to the corresponding source property.

example.title: Keep reactivity after destructuring
example.code:
import { reactive, toRefs } from 'vue'

const state = reactive({ count: 0, label: 'Clicks' })
const { count, label } = toRefs(state)

count.value++
console.log(label.value, count.value) // Clicks 1
state.count++
console.log(count.value) // 2
example.explanation: Each returned ref stays connected to its matching property in the reactive object.

useCases.title: Return destructurable composable state
useCases.scenario: A composable returns several reactive state properties.

useCases.title: Preserve prop reactivity while destructuring
useCases.scenario: A component needs one or more reactive properties from a props object.

useCases.title: Expose linked refs
useCases.scenario: Code needs ref-style access to properties of a reactive object.

interview.question: What does toRefs do?
interview.answer: toRefs takes a reactive object and returns a plain object. Each property in the returned object is a ref connected to the matching source property.
interview.followUp: What happens if the source property does not exist yet? Use toRef for that single property; it can return a usable ref for an optional property.

interview.question: Why use toRefs in a composable?
interview.answer: It preserves reactivity when a composable returns an object that the caller will destructure or spread. The caller reads each returned property through .value in JavaScript.
interview.followUp: Why not return the reactive object directly? Destructuring a reactive object can separate local variables from the reactive property links.

interview.question: How are the refs created?
interview.answer: toRefs is declared for an object and returns refs for its keys. Internally, each ref is made with toRef, so the source property and ref remain synchronized.
interview.followUp: When should toRef be preferred? Use it when only one property is needed or when the property may be optional.

Every returned ref points to the matching property in the original object.

interview.question: What does Vue's `Transition` component do?
interview.answer: `Transition` is a built-in Vue component for enter and leave effects on one element or component. It can react to `v-if`, `v-show`, dynamic components, or a changed `key`.
interview.followUp: How can Vue know when a CSS effect ends? It detects transition or animation events, or you can set `type` or an explicit `duration`.

interview.question: Which CSS classes does `Transition` use?
interview.answer: Vue applies six CSS class stages: enter-from, enter-active, enter-to, leave-from, leave-active, and leave-to. The active classes are useful for defining duration, delay, and easing.
interview.followUp: How would you use a different class prefix? Pass `name="fade"`; Vue then generates classes such as `fade-enter-active`.

interview.question: How do you control replacement timing for dynamic components?
interview.answer: Use `mode="out-in"` to finish the old view before inserting the new one. The other supported modes are `in-out` and the default simultaneous behavior.
interview.followUp: When is `duration` useful? Use it when nested transitions mean the first root event does not represent the complete effect.

Wrap the changing content in `Transition` to animate insertion and removal.

gotchas: The default slot must contain one element or component.
For JavaScript-only effects, disable CSS detection and call `done` in both enter and leave hooks.
For nested effects, set `duration` to include the inner element's delay and animation time.

interview.question: What problem does TransitionGroup solve?
interview.answer: TransitionGroup is for animating insertion, removal, and order changes in a list. It applies transition classes to individual list children, not to the group container.
interview.followUp: How do you animate reordered items? Add the move class and make its CSS transform transitionable. Vue can then animate the changed positions using FLIP.

interview.question: How does TransitionGroup differ from Transition?
interview.answer: Unlike Transition, TransitionGroup can render a list of elements or components. It accepts tag for an optional wrapper, requires unique keys on all children, and does not support transition modes.
interview.followUp: What happens if tag is omitted? The component renders without a wrapper element, so the children are not placed inside an extra DOM container.

interview.question: How do move transitions work?
interview.answer: Use the move class for position changes. If leaving elements remain in normal layout flow, they can prevent Vue from calculating the other items' movement correctly.
interview.followUp: How can the move class name be changed? Pass a custom class through the moveClass prop, written as move-class in a template.

interview.question: What does unref() do?
interview.answer: unref() accepts a value or a ref and always returns the underlying value. For a ref, it reads .value; for another value, it returns that value unchanged.
interview.followUp: How does unref() differ from toValue()? toValue() also calls a getter, while unref() only unwraps refs.

interview.question: What is the TypeScript signature of unref()?
interview.answer: Its type is function unref<T>(ref: T | Ref<T>): T. This lets a function accept either T or Ref<T> and use the result as T.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful in composables? It lets callers pass static values or refs without separate handling code.

interview.question: When should code use unref()?
interview.answer: Use unref() when the input can be a ref or a plain value and you need the plain value. Use isRef() instead when you need to know whether the input is a ref.
interview.followUp: What should be used when getters must also be supported? Use toValue(), because it normalizes values, refs, and getters.

useAttrs.explanation: useAttrs() gives a component access to attributes and event listeners that are not declared in its props or emits. In script setup, use it when the setup context is not available. The returned object has the latest values, but Vue does not make it reactive.

interview.answer: useAttrs() returns the current component's fallthrough attributes. These are attributes and v-on listeners that are not declared in props or emits.
interview.followUp: How would you react to an attribute change? Use a prop instead, because the attrs object is not reactive; onUpdated() can run side effects using the latest values.

interview.question: When should useAttrs() be used?
interview.answer: It is mainly for script setup, where the setup context is not directly available. In a normal setup function, the same data is available as ctx.attrs.
interview.followUp: What is another way to access it in an Options API component? Use the instance property $attrs.

interview.question: What are fallthrough attributes?
interview.answer: Fallthrough attributes commonly include class, style, id, and undeclared event listeners. Vue automatically adds them to a single root element.

interview.question: What does `v-model` do?
interview.answer: `v-model` connects form state to a form element with two-way synchronization. For text inputs and textareas it uses `value` and `input`; for checkboxes and radios it uses `checked` and `change`; selects use `value` and `change`.

interview.followUp: What happens with an option such as `<option :value="{ number: 123 }">`? Selecting it sets the model to that object value.

interview.question: Which `v-model` modifiers are documented?
interview.answer: `.number` converts a valid input string to a number, and `.trim` removes surrounding whitespace. `.lazy` changes synchronization from `input` to `change`.
interview.followUp: What is a limitation of checkbox `true-value` and `false-value`? They do not change the HTML value used for form submission, so radios are needed when one of two submitted values must always be sent.

interview.answer: Vue can patch list elements in place by default. A unique primitive `:key` tells Vue which item each node represents, so it can reuse and reorder nodes correctly.
interview.followUp: When can the default behavior be acceptable? It is suitable for simple output without component state or temporary DOM state such as form values.

interview.question: What happens when v-if and v-for are used together?
interview.answer: v-if has higher priority than v-for on the same node, so the v-if expression cannot use the v-for alias. Move v-for to a wrapping `<template>` or use a computed filtered list.
interview.followUp: How should a list be hidden without filtering it? Put v-if on the container, such as `<ul>` or `<ol>`, instead of on each repeated item.

keyPoints: The loop alias names the current item. Use `in` or `of` as the separator.
For arrays, `(item, index)` provides the value and its zero-based position.
For objects, the loop can expose the value, property name, and index.
With a number, Vue repeats the template that many times, and the loop value starts at 1.
Use `<template v-for>` when each iteration must produce several sibling elements without adding a wrapper element.
When using `<template v-for>`, bind the key to the template rather than to one child element.
gotchas: Avoid putting v-if and v-for on the same element. Put v-for on a wrapping template, or filter the data with a computed property.
Use a unique string or number for :key. Do not use an object as the key.
Copy an array before calling reverse() or sort() in a computed getter, because these methods change the original array.

v-html.summary: Vue directives are special `v-` attributes that update the DOM from JavaScript expressions. They can use arguments, dynamic arguments, and shorthand forms such as `:` and `@`.
v-html.explanation: Vue directives are special attributes that start with `v-`. They apply reactive DOM updates when their expressions change. A directive can also take an argument after `:`. Common shorthand forms are `:` for `v-bind` and `@` for `v-on`.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: The JavaScript expression used by the directive. Its value controls the reactive DOM update.

parameters.name: argument
parameters.description: The directive argument after `:`. It identifies the attribute or event to affect.

v-html.returns: Updates the rendered DOM reactively. For `v-if`, Vue inserts or removes the element based on the expression's truthiness.

example.explanation: This component binds an ID, conditionally renders a paragraph, and inserts trusted HTML.

useCases.scenario: Show or hide an element from a Boolean state.

useCases.title: Dynamic attribute binding
useCases.scenario: Keep HTML attributes such as `id` or `href` synchronized with component data.

useCases.title: Event handling with `v-on`
useCases.scenario: Listen for a DOM event and call a component method.

useCases.title: Raw HTML with `v-html`
useCases.scenario: Render trusted HTML supplied by the application.

interview.question: What is a Vue directive?
interview.answer: A directive is a Vue-provided special attribute whose name starts with `v-`. Its expression is normally a single JavaScript expression, and Vue updates the DOM when that expression changes.
interview.followUp: Which directives are exceptions to the single-expression rule? `v-for`, `v-on`, and `v-slot` are documented exceptions.

interview.question: How do you bind a dynamic HTML attribute?
interview.answer: `v-bind:id="dynamicId"` keeps the element's `id` in sync with `dynamicId`. The shorthand is `:id="dynamicId"`; if the value is `null` or `undefined`, Vue removes the attribute.
interview.followUp: How can the attribute name be computed? Use a dynamic argument such as `:[attributeName]="url"`.

interview.question: What is the difference between interpolation and `v-html`?
interview.answer: Double-mustache interpolation displays data as plain text. `v-html` instead replaces an element's `innerHTML` with the value and interprets it as HTML.
interview.followUp: What is the safe rule for `v-html`? Use it only for trusted content, never for user-provided content.

keyPoints: Vue templates use HTML syntax to connect rendered DOM to component data.
Use `{{ value }}` for reactive text interpolation.
Built-in directives use names that begin with `v-`.
Directive expressions drive reactive DOM updates.
The part after `:` is the directive argument, such as `href` in `v-bind:href`.
Use `@event` as shorthand for `v-on:event`.
Square brackets create a dynamic directive argument, such as `:[attributeName]`.
gotchas: Do not pass user input to `v-html`. Rendering arbitrary HTML can create XSS vulnerabilities.
Use `v-bind` or its `:` shorthand for dynamic attributes. Do not put `{{ }}` inside an HTML attribute.
Content inserted with `v-html` is treated as HTML, and bindings inside that inserted HTML do not run.

v-if.summary: Use `v-if` to render content only when a condition is truthy. Use `v-else-if` and `v-else` for branches, or `v-show` to keep content in the DOM and toggle its display.
v-if.explanation: Vue evaluates the expression on `v-if`. A truthy result creates the block; a falsy result removes it. Use `v-else-if` and `v-else` for the other branches. Use `v-show` when the element should stay in the DOM and only change its CSS display value.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: The expression is evaluated for truthiness.

v-if.returns: Conditionally renders an element or template fragment.

example.title: Toggle conditional content
example.explanation: The button changes the condition. Vue renders one paragraph or the other.

useCases.title: Conditional content
useCases.scenario: Render a component or element only when required data or state is available.

useCases.title: Multiple branches
useCases.scenario: Choose one result from several conditions.

useCases.title: Frequent visibility changes
useCases.scenario: Show and hide an existing element many times.

useCases.title: Grouped elements
useCases.scenario: Toggle several sibling elements as one conditional block.

interview.question: How does `v-if` work?
interview.answer: `v-if` conditionally renders a block. Vue creates it only when the expression is truthy and destroys it when the condition becomes false.
interview.followUp: When is `v-if` lazy? It is lazy when the initial condition is false: Vue does not render the block until the condition first becomes true.

interview.question: What is the difference between `v-if` and `v-show`?
interview.answer: `v-show` always renders the element and keeps it in the DOM. It changes the element's `display` CSS property instead.
interview.followUp: Which directive suits frequent toggles? Usually `v-show`, because it has lower toggle cost after the initial render.

interview.question: How do conditional branches work?
interview.answer: `v-else-if` adds another branch to a `v-if` chain, and `v-else` provides the final branch. Both must immediately follow a valid preceding conditional element.
interview.followUp: Can these branches group several elements? Yes. Put the directive on `<template>`; the wrapper is not included in the rendered result.

keyPoints: `v-if` renders its block only when its expression is truthy.
Use `v-else-if` to add another condition to a `v-if` chain.
Use `v-if` on `<template>` to conditionally group multiple elements without adding a wrapper.
`v-show` keeps the element rendered and changes its `display` style.
Choose based on frequency: `v-show` is suited to frequent toggles, while `v-if` suits conditions that rarely change.
gotchas: Place `v-else` directly after its matching conditional element, or Vue will not recognize it.
Each `v-else-if` must directly follow `v-if` or another `v-else-if`.
Avoid putting `v-if` and `v-for` on one element. Their precedence can make the result unclear.

v-memo.summary: v-memo caches a template subtree and skips its updates when all dependency values are unchanged. It is mainly for measured performance problems in large subtrees or lists.
v-memo.explanation: v-memo stores a template subtree and compares a fixed-length dependency array on later renders. If every dependency is unchanged, Vue skips updates and can reuse the subtree's virtual DOM nodes. Use it only when profiling shows a large, performance-sensitive subtree or list needs this optimization.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: A fixed-length array of values used to decide whether the memoized subtree must update.

example.title: Memoize list items
example.code: ID: {{ item.id }}
example.explanation: This reuses each item's rendered subtree until its selected state changes.

useCases.title: Optimize a large v-for list
useCases.scenario: A large repeated list has expensive item subtrees, and most items remain unchanged when state updates.

useCases.title: Skip stable subtree updates
useCases.scenario: A component contains a costly subtree whose output depends on a small set of values.

interview.question: What does v-memo do?
interview.answer: v-memo memoizes a subtree on an element or component. Vue compares the values in its fixed-length dependency array with the previous render. If all values match, Vue skips updates for that subtree.
interview.followUp: What happens with `v-memo="[]"`? It is effectively the same as `v-once`, because no dependency can invalidate the memoized subtree.

interview.question: When is v-memo useful?
interview.answer: Use `v-memo` when a large subtree or list is expensive to update and most of its content stays unchanged. A common case is a `v-for` list with more than 1000 items.
interview.followUp: How can it help a selectable list? Memoize each item with a dependency such as `[item.id === selected]`, so only items whose selected state changed update.

interview.question: How should the memo dependencies be chosen?
interview.answer: The dependency array must contain the values that affect the subtree's rendered result. In a keyed `v-for`, Vue can infer the item ID from `:key`, so the ID does not need to be repeated in the memo array.
interview.followUp: What is the risk of omitting a changing dependency? Vue may reuse stale output because it skips an update that should have occurred.

keyPoints: The directive caches a template subtree for later renders.
You can place v-memo on a normal element or on a component.
Its value must be a fixed-length array whose entries represent the subtree's update conditions.
When all dependencies stay equal, Vue skips updates for the whole memoized subtree.
Vue may reuse the previous virtual DOM nodes instead of creating them again.
Large repeated lists are the main documented use case.
gotchas: Wrong dependencies can prevent updates that should happen. Keep the dependency array fixed in length and include every value that can change the subtree's output.
Do not use this directive by default. It is intended for small optimizations in code where rendering performance is a measured problem.
An empty dependency list makes the subtree behave like v-once, so it will not update after the initial render.

v-model.summary: v-model synchronizes form controls with JavaScript state. It supports text fields, textareas, checkboxes, radios, and selects, with modifiers for common input handling.
v-model.explanation: v-model keeps a form control and JavaScript state synchronized. Vue chooses the matching DOM property and event for text inputs, checkboxes, radio buttons, select elements, and textareas. The JavaScript state is the source of truth, and modifiers can change when or how input is stored.

example.title: Form controls with v-model
example.explanation: This binds three form controls to reactive state. The modifiers trim text and convert valid numeric input.
