useCases.scenario: Keep a text field or textarea synchronized with reactive state.

useCases.title: Checkbox groups
useCases.scenario: Collect one or more checked choices.

useCases.title: Select controls
useCases.scenario: Let a user choose one or several options.

useCases.title: Input modifiers
useCases.scenario: Convert or clean input while it is stored.

interview.question: How does v-model work on native form controls?
interview.answer: v-model is shorthand for binding the control's value and listening for its update event. Text inputs and textareas use value plus input; checkboxes and radios use checked plus change; selects use value plus change.
interview.followUp: How does this differ on a component? The binding uses a modelValue prop and an update:modelValue event by default.

interview.question: What values can checkbox bindings store?
interview.answer: A checkbox bound to a boolean stores true or false. Several checkboxes can share an array or Set, which then contains the values of the checked boxes.
interview.followUp: How can a checkbox store values other than true and false? Use true-value and false-value, though these do not change the submitted HTML value.

interview.question: What do the built-in v-model modifiers do?
interview.answer: The .lazy modifier listens for change instead of input. The .number modifier converts a parsable input string with parseFloat(), while .trim removes surrounding whitespace.
interview.followUp: What happens when .number receives an empty input? It stores an empty string, rather than the result of DOM valueAsNumber.

keyPoints: Use v-model instead of writing a value binding and an input or change handler by hand.
The directive works with input controls, textarea, and select elements.
Checkboxes and radio buttons bind through checked and change rather than value and input.
Create select options from reactive data with v-for and bind each option's value dynamically.
Use v-bind on radio, checkbox, and option values to bind objects, numbers, booleans, or other non-string values.
A number input automatically gets number-style conversion, even without writing the modifier.
gotchas: Set initial form values in JavaScript, not with HTML value, checked, or selected attributes.
During IME composition, v-model does not update. Use your own input listener and value binding when those intermediate updates are needed.
For a select, use a disabled option with an empty value when the initial state has no matching option, especially for iOS.

v-on.summary: v-on listens for events and runs a method or inline statement. Its shorthand is @.
v-on.explanation: Use v-on to listen for an event and run code when it happens. The @ form is shorthand. You can call a component method, write a short inline statement, or use modifiers to change the event behavior.

parameters.name: event
parameters.description: The event to listen for, such as click or keyup.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: A method name, inline statement, or an object of event and listener pairs.

v-on.returns: Not applicable; v-on attaches an event listener.

example.title: Handle a click
example.code: Count: {{ count }}
example.explanation: This button uses the short form of v-on to run an inline statement when clicked.

useCases.title: Inline action
useCases.scenario: A button changes a reactive value when clicked.

useCases.title: Prevent default submission
useCases.scenario: A form should not reload the page after submission.

useCases.title: Listen for a custom event
useCases.scenario: A component parent handles an event emitted by a child.

useCases.title: Use event modifiers
useCases.scenario: A handler should run only once or only for a specific key.

interview.question: What is v-on used for?
interview.answer: v-on attaches an event listener. Its long form is v-on:event and its shorthand is @event. It accepts a method handler or an inline statement.
interview.followUp: How can an inline handler receive the event? Use the special $event value, such as @click="handle('ok', $event)".

interview.question: How do method and inline handlers receive events?
interview.answer: A method handler points to a component method, and Vue passes the native DOM Event as its only argument. An inline handler can use $event when it needs that object.
interview.followUp: What does event.target provide? It identifies the element that dispatched the event, so the handler can inspect that element.

interview.question: What are event modifiers?
interview.answer: Modifiers add common event behavior without putting DOM details in the method. For example, .stop stops propagation, .prevent cancels the default action, and .once limits handling to one time.
interview.followUp: When should .passive be used? It is commonly used for touch listeners so the browser can perform its default behavior without waiting for the handler.

keyPoints: Use v-on, or its shorter @ form, to listen for events.
An inline handler runs a JavaScript statement when the event occurs.
A method handler names a component method that Vue should call.
Method handlers receive the native DOM event as their argument.
The event name appears after v-on:, such as v-on:click or @click.
On a component, v-on listens for custom events emitted by the child.
gotchas: Do not combine .passive with .prevent. Passive listeners tell the browser that the handler will not cancel the event.
Modifier order changes behavior. For example, .prevent.self and .self.prevent do not prevent the same clicks.
The object form can map events to handlers, but modifiers cannot be added to that form.

v-once.summary: v-once renders an element or component only once. Vue skips that subtree during later updates.
v-once.explanation: Add v-once to an element or component when its rendered content should stay fixed after the first render. Vue treats that whole subtree as static during later renders, including its children.

useCases.title: Freeze initial content
useCases.scenario: A value is needed when the component first renders but never changes afterward.

useCases.title: Reduce update work
useCases.scenario: A large static section is inside a component that updates often.

useCases.title: Keep list items static
useCases.scenario: Each item in a rendered list is fixed after its first render.

interview.question: What does v-once do?
interview.answer: v-once renders an element or component one time and skips it during future updates. The whole subtree, including child content, is treated as static.
interview.followUp: How would you freeze only when selected values stay unchanged? Use v-memo with a fixed-length dependency array and make sure every required dependency is included.

interview.question: When is v-once useful?
interview.answer: It can improve update performance by preventing Vue from processing a subtree again. This is useful when runtime data is needed for the first render but never needs to change afterward.
interview.followUp: What is the related directive for conditional skipping? v-memo conditionally skips updates when all dependency values match the previous render.

interview.question: Where can v-once be used?
interview.answer: You can put v-once on a single element, an element with children, a component, or an element used with v-for. It has no expression.
interview.followUp: What must be checked when using memoization in a list? With v-memo, use it on the same element as v-for and provide correct dependencies.

keyPoints: Use v-once to render an element or component only once.
The directive freezes the complete subtree, not just the element carrying the directive.
It can reduce work during later component updates.
For conditional update skipping, use the related v-memo directive instead.
gotchas: Do not use it for content that must react to later state changes. The element, component, and all children will stop updating.
v-once accepts no expression. Place it directly on the element or component you want to freeze.

v-show.summary: `v-show` controls an element's visibility from an expression. It keeps the element rendered and changes its CSS `display` style instead of creating or removing the element.
v-show.explanation: `v-show` keeps the element rendered and in the DOM. Vue controls its inline `display` style from the truthiness of the expression. Use it when the element needs frequent visibility changes, because toggling is cheaper than creating and destroying the element.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: Any value. Vue uses whether the value is truthy or falsy.

example.title: Toggle an element's visibility
example.code: Hello!
example.explanation: The heading stays in the DOM while Vue changes its CSS display value when isVisible changes.

useCases.scenario: A panel is opened and closed many times during one page session.

useCases.title: Preserve mounted content
useCases.scenario: A form section should stay mounted while temporarily hidden.

useCases.title: Simple visibility changes
useCases.scenario: A loading or help message needs simple CSS-based visibility control.

interview.question: How does `v-show` work?
interview.answer: `v-show` always renders the element and keeps it in the DOM. It changes the element's CSS `display` property to show or hide it.
interview.followUp: When is `v-if` usually a better choice? Use `v-if` when the condition rarely changes, because it avoids the initial rendering cost when the condition starts false.

interview.question: What is the difference between `v-if` and `v-show`?
interview.answer: Both directives can control visibility, but they use different strategies. `v-if` creates and destroys the block, while `v-show` keeps it rendered and changes CSS.
interview.followUp: Which directive is better for frequent toggles? Usually `v-show`, because repeated toggles do not recreate the block.

interview.question: What does the `v-show` expression control?
interview.answer: The expression is evaluated for truthiness. A truthy value makes the element visible, and a falsy value causes Vue to hide it with the `display` style.
interview.followUp: Can `v-show` control several sibling elements as one block? No. Use `v-if` on a `<template>` when you need a conditional group.

keyPoints: `v-show` displays the element when its expression is truthy and hides it otherwise.
Vue uses an inline `display` style to control visibility.
The element is rendered even when hidden and remains available in the DOM.
Unlike lazy `v-if`, `v-show` renders the element during the initial render.
Choose `v-show` for UI elements that change visibility frequently.
gotchas: You cannot use `v-show` on `<template>` or combine it with `v-else`.
`v-show` renders at startup, so it can cost more initially than `v-if`.

v-slot.summary: v-slot provides content for a component's named or default slots. It can also receive props from a child slot, including through destructuring.
v-slot.explanation: Use v-slot to provide content for a component's named or default slots. The child places that content with slot outlets. A slot can also pass props to the parent, which reads them through the v-slot value.

parameters.description: Optional slot name, such as header; it defaults to default.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Optional JavaScript expression that receives slot props.

interview.question: What does v-slot do?
interview.answer: v-slot marks content for a named or scoped slot. Use it on a template for named slots, or directly on a component for a single default scoped slot. The # prefix is its shorthand.
interview.followUp: How do you pass data back to slot content? Put bindings such as :item on the child’s slot outlet, then read the resulting object through v-slot.

interview.question: How are named and default slots provided?
interview.answer: A named slot uses a slot name, such as v-slot:header or #header. Content without a template wrapper is implicitly assigned to the default slot when named slots are also present.
interview.followUp: What changes when the default slot also receives props? Use an explicit <template #default="props"> so its scope is clear.

interview.question: How do scoped slots pass data?
interview.answer: The child passes attributes on its <slot> outlet as slot props. The parent receives those props through v-slot and can use normal JavaScript destructuring, such as v-slot="{ text, count }".
interview.followUp: Can slot names be dynamic? Yes. Use v-slot:[dynamicSlotName], while following dynamic directive argument syntax rules.

keyPoints: v-slot supplies content to a named slot or receives data from a scoped slot.
The slot argument selects the destination; without one, the slot is named default.
A child can expose values through its slot outlet, and the parent reads them from v-slot.
The v-slot value supports JavaScript destructuring for concise access to slot props.
gotchas: When named slots and a scoped default slot are used together, put the default slot on an explicit template element.
Do not use a variable declared as the slot scope inside that slot's dynamic name.
v-slot does not support modifiers.

v-text.explanation: `v-text` sets an element's `textContent` to the value of its expression. This replaces all content already inside the element. Use text interpolation when only part of existing text should change.

interview.question: What does v-text do?
interview.answer: `v-text` updates an element's text content from an expression. It sets the element's `textContent` property.
interview.followUp: How can you update only part of the text? Use mustache interpolation, such as `Count: {{count}}`.

interview.question: What value does v-text expect?
interview.answer: The directive expects a string expression. Vue evaluates the expression and uses its value as the element's text content.
interview.followUp: What happens to existing child elements? They are overwritten because `textContent` replaces the element's contents.

interview.followUp: When is interpolation better? Use it when static text and a changing value must appear together.

Vue implements the directive by assigning to the DOM `textContent` property.
Choose interpolation when only one part of the text should change.
Mustache interpolation lets other text remain in the same element.
gotchas: Do not use it when the element must keep other child content. It replaces that content.

watchEffect.summary: watch() runs a callback when one or more chosen reactive sources change. It gives explicit control over the source, callback timing, initial run, nested changes, and cleanup.
watchEffect.explanation: watch() observes one or more reactive sources and calls a callback when the selected source changes. Unlike watchEffect(), it does not automatically track values read inside the callback. Options can run it immediately, detect nested changes, control timing, or run it only once.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: A ref, getter, reactive object, or array of these sources to observe.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Runs when the source changes. Receives new value, old value, and a cleanup registration function.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings: immediate, deep, flush, onTrack, onTrigger, and once.

watchEffect.returns: A WatchHandle that is callable to stop the watcher. It also provides pause(), resume(), and stop() methods.

useCases.title: Explicit state reactions
useCases.scenario: Run a side effect only for selected state changes.

interview.question: How does watch() differ from watchEffect()?
interview.answer: watch() tracks only the source passed to it and calls the callback when that source changes. It provides the current and previous values, so the callback can compare them.
interview.followUp: How would you watch several sources? Pass an array of refs or getters. The callback receives matching arrays of new and old values.

interview.question: What does immediate: true do?
interview.answer: immediate: true runs the callback when the watcher is created, before a source change. The old value is undefined on that first call.
interview.followUp: When is watchEffect() simpler? Use it when the callback already reads the reactive values it should track, because it tracks those dependencies automatically and runs immediately.

interview.question: How should a watcher cancel stale asynchronous work?
interview.answer: A watcher can register cleanup with the callback's onCleanup function or with onWatcherCleanup() in Vue 3.5+. Cleanup runs before the watcher runs again, so it can cancel stale asynchronous work.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies to onWatcherCleanup()? It must run during synchronous callback execution, so register it before an await.

keyPoints: Use watch() when a specific ref, getter, or reactive object should control when a side effect runs.
Compared with watchEffect(), watch() gives explicit source selection and does not run until a watched source changes by default.
Set immediate: true when the first callback run should happen during watcher setup.
Set deep: true to react to nested mutations from an object source. Vue 3.5+ also accepts a number for maximum traversal depth.
Set once: true when the watcher should stop automatically after its first callback execution. This option requires Vue 3.4 or newer.
gotchas: Call onWatcherCleanup() before any await in an async watcher. It cannot be registered after the function has paused at await.
A getter watches its returned value, not every nested mutation. Use deep: true when nested changes should trigger the callback.
Use flush: 'sync' carefully. Avoid it for data such as arrays that can be changed many times in one synchronous sequence.
Create watchers synchronously when possible. A watcher made later in an asynchronous callback must be stopped manually.
